title: 40k Badcast 192 - Talk About Double Fisting!
content:
The Tabletop Battles group is made up of dozens of multi-talented authors, many of whom have other projects outside of the site. In addition to their work here, Dan Boyd and Campbell "SRM" McLaughlin have their own podcast, the 40K Badcast, a member of the Tabletop Battles Media Network.

Friends, it's that time again! The Badcast has returned with a slew of new, hot bullshit for you to pump directly into your brain! In this show, Campbell bullies his friend via text, Dan takes the listeners to business school, and the fellas break down the new Marine codex! Also, Campbell once again proves to be emotionally unavailable in the face of real affection. It would be sad if we could still feel things. Alas. Enjoy!

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Tomb Kings Reinforcements of Nehekhara Box
content:
If you’ve ever been to the city of Vienna, my adopted home, and visited the Cathedral of St Stephen, you might have chanced to go into the undercroft with an enthusiastic old tour guide. The tour progresses through the Imperial Crypt, which houses the viscera (but not the bones or hearts; those are elsewhere) of the ruling Habsburg family going back hundreds of years, and into the catacombs that wind beneath the centre of the imperial city - therein you’ll find the earthly remains of about ten thousand people, buried below the cathedral before Emperor Joseph II stopped the practise in 1783. To say there are a lot of bones might be an understatement.

Skeleton Chariot - Credit: keewa

This new Tomb Kings box is not quite as bone-dense as the catacombs beneath St Stephen's, but even so, it feels like an overwhelming osseous onslaught. The bones… the bones! There are so many of them. The box is titled Reinforcements of Nehekhara and contains a skull-spinning 78 models.

Broken down, the set comprises:

  • 36 Skeleton Warriors
  • 36 Skeleton Archers
  • 6 Skeleton Chariots

That is a lot of bone boys. Notably, there are no characters in this set; it’s purely a big box of bodies to beef up your already existing Tomb Kings of Khemri army.

Skeleton Warriors - Credit: keewa

Building

The skeleton warriors go together relatively easily; they’re pretty much absent of customisation beyond “do you want spears or khopesh swords?” and “which shield would you like?” This might otherwise be a bit of a bummer, but since they’re literally faceless grunts, I don’t think people will be too frustrated by it, though I would have preferred some head-swap options.

As usual with blocks of infantry,  you have the option to include a champion with either a sword or an axe, a musician (with a nice Roman-style cornu), and an icon bearer (with two different icons to choose from, for a bit of variety). The models go together easily enough; each one is only a handful of parts, nicely bucking the GW trend of having very parts-dense monopose models. Despite my job, I am still quite a slow builder, but I managed to chuck together thirty-odd skeletons in an evening while watching TV. Compared to the venerable old Tomb Kings models, these definitely feel like a massive upgrade; the detail is as crisp as a winter morning, but the apparent desire to render the skeletons more “realistically” (i.e, in proper scale, with bones that aren’t the same width as a human arm) does result in models that feel a bit spindly and fragile at times. I had a few breakages on the sprue, mostly of lower legs, and while they’re relatively easy to correct, it’s still a bit of a bummer.

The iconic Tomb Kings tower shields retain their very distinctive shape and look great; there’s very little to complain about there… although it would have been nice to have more blank shields to choose from. Since GW has provided us with a very nice Khemri transfer sheet replete with hieroglyphs, it’s a shame that we don’t have more space to use them; that’s a very minor quibble, though.

The archers aren’t massively different to the warriors; again, you have the same options of a champion (confusingly, one of the champions is holding a long horn, but I don’t think he’s supposed to be a musician), a musician (this time with a very cute little drum) and an icon-bearer (with two different icons, either a small roundel with a piece of cloth, or a long cartouche-looking thing). The main difference between archers and warriors is that the archers are unarmoured and carry quivers on their backs (the special characters have a quiver and a bow neatly strapped to their backs), which are separate pieces and in my fat-fingered world, it’s quite annoying to get them positioned just so without feeling like the pressure I’m applying is going to obliterate these poor things at the ankle.

Unlike the warriors, the archers do have switchable heads, which is nice but raises the question as to why the warriors don’t.

The chariots have exactly the same choices as the rest: champion, musician, banner; you know the drill by now. The charioteers can also be assembled with bows or spears, the drivers have veils over their faces, presumably to protect their non-existent lungs from all that dust, and one of the drivers can have a rather gnarly-looking whip, which presumably doesn’t do much to skeleton horses. In addition, the champion’s chariot has the option of some nice wings for a little extra bling. The kit goes together nicely, with only minimal fuss. I had a little trouble keeping the horses level while the glue dried to hold them into the yoke, but it was easy enough to fix with a little light manipulation. I kept the driver and champion separate for ease of painting, and when it comes time to put them in place, there are some handy slots in the wickerwork floor, which I greatly appreciated.

Skeleton Warriors - Credit: keewa

The reinforcements box comes with a pair of transfer sheets - the first available TK transfers for The Old World, featuring a bevvy of symbols for each of the Nehekharan deities, plus a bunch of extra hieroglyphs to make your own curses and add plenty of Ancient Egyptian flair to the models. I’ve already said it, but it would have been nice to have enough bare shields to give every model in a unit a shield with a nice large transfer on it.

To an Old World neophyte like me, this box is probably not the ideal introduction, but for old hands who already own a Tomb Kings army and want to either supplement it with more bodies, or to swap their old, tired-looking Skeletons with these new, updated versions, it’s probably a must-have. The models are detailed and crisp, and they're characterful and easy to paint quickly to boot. The chariots in particular stand out as a massive upgrade from the old bone chariots, really showcasing how far model design and production has come in the last two decades.

The Reinforcements of Nehekhara set won’t be around forever: it’s a limited-time product, so if you're interested, grab it sooner rather than later. The contents will certainly be parceled out into separate kits later, so you'll be able to pick them up even if you miss the boat on the Nehekhara box.

title: The Roguelike Roundup, 10/10 - 10/24
content:
In the Roguelike Roundup, Jake sifts through the deluge of roguelikes and autobattlers that come out every week (or slightly longer) to shout out the ones he thinks are worth your time.

Dicevaders

Dicevaders is a charming Balatro-like (you try to beat a set score through the use of multipliers and various scoring tricks). You play as aliens invading the solar system, with each planet acting as a level to clear. This framing gives them the ability to design characters with interesting aesthetics and mechanics, and they take full advantage of that fact. If you clear a level in one go, you’re even rewarded with a cute animation unique to the character (my favorite is the blob girl who puts the planet in a jelly cube).

The game begins simply: roll 3 dice, put units in numbered lanes that score when you roll that number. Pairs and triples are good. While initially I was skeptical of the depth I was very quickly proven wrong. The artifacts you can equip offer a wide range of game-changing effects and also can level up through gameplay. In fact, there are entire archetypes revolving around generating experience for your artifacts.

Instead of standard ascension-style difficulties the game is split into chapters that have new bosses. I found this really refreshing, as playing the same content but it’s just a bit harder is dull in my opinion.

After each turn, you visit a shop which allows you to purchase generic upgrades like budges which move a die one up or down, chrono which rerolls dice, extra tiles, experience for your relics, and units. The money you don't spend doesn't stay with you and instead turns into bonus dice for the next round. Additionally, finishing a round early gives you the ability to level up the shop. This is a brilliant system which gives the player total freedom to farm units, or rush for the rarer stuff by winstreaking.

Progression in a roguelike is a tricky thing. Too much too fast and the player exhausts all the options. Too slow and the player gets bored. Dicevaders nails it, giving you a new character or artifacts after basically every run. In addition, each character unlocks specific perks that make their gameplay more interesting, so there’s lots of incentive to play each character over and over.

The score thresholds are tuned perfectly. Somehow, you go from needing 100 points round one to 150 million in the final round and it never feels like too much or too little to ask of you.

In addition, after you ‘complete’ the game, you unlock a new mode filled with unique modifiers, artifacts, and upgrades. There is so much content here and I keep coming back for more. I set aside four hours to give as thorough a review as I could and now I’m nearing nineteen hours in the game.

There's also a plethora of quality-of-life features like the ability to rewind a turn, an extensive strategy guide that unlocks more the deeper you go and speed up features. The visual scoring effects are satisfying in the same vein as the addicting Balatro cha-ching and the whole game is made in a cute retro theme like Scott Pilgrim meets Space Invaders.

This game is a complete experience made by a developer who absolutely knows what they’re doing, and it gets a strong endorsement from me.

Tower Tactics 2

I had a lovely time with Tower Tactics: Liberation so I was thrilled to see this pop up in early access.

Tower Tactics’ special sauce comes from the combination of deckbuilding and tower defense. Placing towers isn’t as simple as other tower defense games where you have a constant set of options to choose from. Here your towers are cards in the deck, and every round you’ll draw a hand of them. In typical autobattler fashion, placing three of a tower will fuse into a higher-level tower. Three of those upgrade to the next level, and so on. In lieu of towers costing money, they cost mana. Holding off on placing towers in early rounds allows you to build up your mana pool to afford bigger and better towers.

There are several game modes that return from the original game. You have your standard round-based tower defense, as well as a timer-based one where enemies constantly spawn and you gain mana cards every twenty or so seconds. Additionally, there’s a mode where you get to craft your own map, building routes for enemies to travel down. This mode is the most interesting one, as the other two tend to generate maps with a single lane, leading to stale gameplay rounds.

The initial towers you have access to aren’t going to blow your socks off. You have your bomb launcher, your default rapid fire tower, your slow hitting tower that stuns, and a few that riff off those ideas. However, as you rapidly unlock the other characters and upgrades, things start getting interesting. Towers that supercharge on certain squares, ones that teleport around the map and ricochet shots everywhere, and spell generation keeps each run interesting. Unfortunately, the trinkets are, for the most part, generic stat upgrades. Getting 10% more attack speed is good, but it’s not necessarily exciting.

Being able to freely adjust tower placement between rounds sounds nice in theory, but in practice it means there are no consequences for misplacing and thus no tension in the decision. Coupled with the fact that your mana sink is not in upgrading towers, but simply placing more of them, and most missions will end the same way: as many towers as you can place directly in the center of the map.

The feedback the towers give you feels good. The damage numbers popping up scratch that itch in the back of your mind, and the game has a solid tutorial that brings you up to pace quickly. The game never leaves you guessing on any esoteric stats, and being able to upgrade base stats that affect you and all your towers is interesting.

The other positive is the developer, who updates their game constantly and is always taking player feedback into account. Since writing this review, the game has already been updated five times with adjustments and bug fixes.

There’s also an incremental game built in, the new crystal mine mode. Incrementals are not really my thing, and it doesn’t seem to loop back into the core gameplay, but it’s there if you want it.

Burn With Me

A more story-driven roguelike than I am usually drawn to, Burn With Me has a hand-drawn style that gives an Edgar-Allen-Poe-If-He-Was-A-Furry vibe and a thematically satisfying gameplay loop. Use the demons you have to summon more demons, chasing that infernal power into the Faustian bargain at the end of the line. Beat the score for the round by enough, and you’ll bank some points that can bail you out later on.

True to its source material, every action in this game costs something. Drawing a card removes a random one in your hand from the game. Certain cards will destroy themselves after being played, or prey upon their neighbors in the pentagram.

Unless they don’t. That’s the trick the game doesn’t tell you. There’s always a way around these prices. You don’t burn a card when you draw if you don’t have any in hand. You don’t siphon power if you play the siphon card first. This subtle game design kept me going as each chapter shows you a new damned character with their own literal personal demons to go up against and accompanying bespoke mechanics. The final chapter combines all of the mechanics and characters in a really challenging and satisfying conclusion, both mechanically and thematically.

The soundtrack is a mellow, jazzy track with lots of piano. It doesn’t overstate itself, but it gives rainy-day-at-the-cafe vibes that I really enjoy. There’s also a rotoscoped hand that has a shocking amount of personality while you play. It beckons you to pick up cards, gives thumbs up when you do well, and literally swats your cursor back to the gameplay if you annoy it with clicks.

While I prefer my demons more horrific than animalistic, the art style is charming, and the little specks of colored detail allow you an easy way to understand what the demons do in broad strokes. Usually, green ones will have some sort of payoff later, while pink ones will deliver big points for big costs.

Overall, this is a game well worth its small price tag and a great way to spend an afternoon or evening. The finale was legitimately challenging, and I had to restart several times to get a run that could get me over the finish line.

title: Welcome to Warcrow
content:
Welcome to Warcrow, friends.

This is Corvus Belli's latest skirmish wargame. Do you like playing Fantasy games but hate the idea of assembling, painting and then transporting more than 50 models to and from your FLGS? Do you like being engaged with the game the entire time instead of turning your brain off during your opponent's turn? Finally, do you take great satisfaction in playing with gorgeous models that can be incredibly easy to paint? This is the game for you.

Thank you to Corvus Belli for providing some of these models and rules for review.

Narrative and Setting

Warcrow - The defenders of Feudom clash with the monstrous Scions (photo courtesy of Musterkrux)

Warcrow is set in the world of Lindwurm, which contains your usual Fantasy tropes. You've got an ancient seemingly extinct progenitor race that did weird, nasty things to the mystic flows of the world and has left it to the following civilisations to clean up. The Moon (one of two) is approaching a period of syzygy (you have no idea how long I have waited to use that word in an appropriate context; we're talking near on decades, people) and with it, the flow of magic within this world is reaching a dangerous peak. The nations and peoples of Lindwurm must contend with The Fog, the physical manifestation of magical corruption that creeps across the land, consuming and corrupting everything it touches.

Factions

Let's take a quick look at the different factions available in the game. You've got: Empire, Bretonnia, Orcs and Goblins, Wood Elves, Dwarves, and Chaos...Sorry, wrong setting. I joke but also, if you want a quick reference for understanding the setting, the Warhammer Fantasy (Pre-Age of Sigmar) parallel isn't wrong.

Hegemony of Embersig

Warcrow - Hegemony of Embersig

The Hegemony is a faction where your demographics is mostly Human but with a dash of Elf and a pinch of Dwarf mixed in (Note to self: 'A Pinch of Dwarf' would be an excellent band name), noting that Embersig is the in-game translation of 'All People' which could be taken as an ambition, promise or threat depending on the time of day. The Hegemony play style is advancing onto objective and holding them with a few well placed ranged weapons (gunpowder is a helluva drug when everyone else is using bows and throwing sharp sticks).

If you're looking for a centre-piece unit for the Hegemony you should consider the War Rig, which is a clockwork robot that stomps around and flattens people with a dragon-shaped hammer-flamethrower combo.

Warcrow - War Rig

Feudom

Warcrow - Feudom

You've got Knights, Peasants and Magical Damsels: This faction is Bretonnia AF and I am entirely here for it. The entire reason this initial Warcrow review has been delayed is because when CB announced the game and the relevant factions I knew, from Day One, what my faction choice would be. So, I didn't even jump into the game proper until they had released enough models for me to play Feudom and pay it the respect it deserves as a faction. So, while CB has indeed sent us some models to assist in reviewing this game, and we thank them for their generosity, I want to stress that I bought into this game before any review content was sent to us because I have a lot of faith in CB being able to deliver on a skirmish wargame with exquisite models. A faith that has, in my opinion, been rewarded.

Warcrow - Feudom (Photo courtesy of Musterkrux)

Feudom's game plan is relatively defensive; the faction is generally pretty good at arriving at a hill (or other notable landmark) and then not dying on it. Maybe this is the hill your opponent's models die on? I mean maybe, I don't care so much, all I know is that my models are here and they're not going anywhere.

A centrepiece or iconic model for this faction would be Roland Loussier and his Griffon, Whitetrail. The only thing cooler than a cavalry charge is a flying cavalry charge. Just look at him, what a heckin' chonker.

Roland Louissier and Whitetrail (photo courtesy of Corvus Belli)

The Northern Tribes

Warcrow - War Riders

Orcs and Varanks (who are not-Orcs, I guess, with blue skin and pronounced lower canines but are definitely not Orcs) live in the far north and are sweeping down from the freezing cold to conquer the other, weaker nations. As far as the character of the faction is concerned, there's a bit of the romanticism of living in touch with nature as a contrast to the industrialisation of nations like Embersig but only a little bit; the Northern Tribes read like they rampage and pillage as a choice more than a necessity.

The Northern Tribes play style is to use their superior offensive capability to offset their weaker objective holding capabilities, they need to push people off objectives because they can't contest them as well.

Sÿenann

Warcrow - Sÿenann

The Sÿenann are the elves that live in, and protect, the Great Forest (stop me if you've heard this one). The Great Forest is pretty rad, in as much as it's not so much a single, monolithic geographical location but it's actually scattered all over Lindwurm, connected via a network of portals. There's a cool side faction of the Sÿenann, the elves who live in the part of the Great Forest that suffered from some sort of mysterious blight, that part of the forest is diseased and dying and this is reflected in the inhabitants of that area: The Ashen. They look absolutely miserable and they look like they're going to make that everyone else's problem.

The Sÿenann play style is high mobility glass cannons playing at hit-and-run tactics with a fair whack of ranged gameplay.

If you're looking for a cool-as-heck unit for the Sÿenann, we recommend you take a gander at Eachann the Great Centaurelf. Does exactly what it says on the box: Half horse, half elf, all angry.

Mounthaven

Warcrow - Mounthaven Dwarves

I'm going to be real with you, you already know what a Dwarf faction in a war game is about. They're short, slow and tough as nails. Some of their magic-users focus on shaping Orichalcum, the precious metal that rests under the surface of Lindwurm. Mounthaven's playstyle is a bit of a Hammer and Anvil affair, your solid basic infantry advance on the enemy and aggressively Not Die while you set up your big hits from the flank.

When it comes to heckin' chonkers, check this guy out. The Waljan the Ancestor (the Last of the First) is a shaped being summoned by the Mounthaven Orichalcum Smiths. Not only does Waljan wreak absolute havoc in your opponent's lines but they also come back after they get put down. We've had one massacre, yes. But what about second massacre?

Warcrow - Waljan

Scions of Yalgometh

Warcrow - Scions of Yaldabaoth (Photo courtesy of Musterkrux)

Remember earlier in the review where we mentioned that the current problems that befall the people of Lindwurm are the result of poor decisions made by an ancient, extinct civilisation? Yeah, well, reports of the death of the Gae Assail are greatly exaggerated*.

Other factions suffer penalties when their magic-users drink too deep of the Fog, the Scions just go full throttle and chug the good stuff like a Fratboy at a Kegger. Corruption is just like Pringles, once you pop you can't stop.

The aesthetics for Scions is amazing. Lots of magic corruption, body horror (not quite Human Centipede levels of people sewing things to other people but that's the direction we're heading here...), and a lovely balance of the bestial and the demonic in both their human followers and their dark overlords. I love that the wannabe Humans who desperately want to ascend go full Buffalo Bill and wear the skins of other animals and even people to emulate their superiors who have undergone genuine transformations.

A great centre-piece for the Scions is actually the grand Master Uruk himself, a leader piece you get in the starter box. Dude is Diablo as hell and I celebrate his Big Red Energy (but, like, classic chunky Diablo-styles, less so stupid, sexy Diablo.).

Warcrow - Master Uruk (Photo courtesy of Musterkrux)

Gameplay Overview

Like Infinity, Warcrow is designed to keep both players engaged with the game as much as possible by providing reactions and decisions to be made by the non-active player during some contested rolls. Your ability to make reactive movements (or even attacks) in the opposing players turn adds a layer of delicious complexity to the game.

Dice Mechanics: Just like an earlier Corvus Belli game, Aristeia (now known as Hexadome Legends), Warcrow uses a proprietary dice system that uses Successes, Blocks, and Special symbols, though now on D8s instead of D6s. The ratio of these symbols is different across various dice. Your Red and Orange dice are more 'Success' focused, your Yellow dice are mostly 'Special' orientated and your Blue, Green and Black dice have the highest proportion of 'Block' symbols. It's also worth noting that there are 'hollow' symbols (where the Shield is just an outline or the Star has a missing 'dot' in the middle), these are only counted under specific circumstances.

Warcrow - So many D8s.

During a standard attack sequence, you and your opponent will roll certain dice (Attackers will usually be using abilities that use more Red, Yellow and Orange dice while Defensive skills are more Blue, Green and Black....but this is not necessarily always true for every character or ability available to them). On one level both players determine how many Hits they are sending at their opponent compared to how many Blocks the respective parties have. It's perfectly possible to have an Attacking model and the Defender both do damage to each other, it's not a Winner-Takes-All resolution system. Then, on top of the potential exchange of damage you have the Switch system, where you can spend your dice results (predominantly Special results but there's often a surcharge of Successes or Blocks you need to cash in, as well) to trigger movement/placement effects or inflict status effects on models (friendly or enemy).

Gameplay Example: Here we have Master Uruk, the big bad dude himself, attacking the noble warrior Morgane of Jauffret. His melee attack roll is one Red die, two Orange and a Yellow. Morgane rolls her Defence stat of two Blue and a Black. You'll notice in the photo that one her 'shield' die results is hollow instead of being entirely filled in/white (we'll cover that in a moment).

Master Uruk attacks Morgane (Warcrow)

Uruk is sending 4 damage (that's the number of hits he's rolled on the dice) but also note that he can use his two Special results (the ! symbols) to negate one of Morgane's Block results.

On the other side, Morgane has rolled three Blocks and two Special results. However, the hollow Block won't count here as they only count for triggering Switches or for Elite characters (Morgane of Jauffret, ex-Priestess of Selas turned Inquisitor? Not quite elite enough.). Sadly, she doesn't have any Switches to use those Special results so she's stopping 2 of Uruk's incoming damage before his Switch negates one of them. So, Morgane is taking 3 damage unless, furthermore, Uruk decides to spend some of his Hits to heal himself up from any damage taken earlier.

Models and Materials

War games are more than just their rules, part of the hobby experience is in the assembly, painting and enjoyment of the physical models. So, let's talk about Warcrow's models as well as the materials they are made out of.

Sculpts

Let's be clear, this is a Corvus Belli game. The sculpt quality is amazing. The proportions are nice, the way they communicate texture on models (Leather, metal armour, corrupted skin), and being a skirmish game CB can indulge more dramatic sculpts within units without worrying about duplicates ruining the look. The crisp details make these models really easy to paint, as well, you can go full Studio styles or toss some Contrasts onto them and let the model do the work.

Materials

Here is, unfortunately, a mild frustration. CB is using two different materials. One appears to be used in the rank and file models while characters or other important/unique models get a different material. Research indicates the first material might be Siocast while the other could be a thermoplastic (if someone can confirm otherwise, please sing out). Siocast has been previously criticised as an unfortunate compromise for managing the cost of materials. A common issue observed is the difficulty in removing mold lines from siocast models. This was certainly true for earlier iterations of siocast but the Warcrow models don't seem to have inherited this problem. However, they remain somewhat 'rubbery' to the touch, thin extremities (swords and bows in particular) flop around something fierce. You could argue that this degree of flexibility is better than rigid brittleness when it comes to surviving bumps and falls. Personally, I wouldn't but that flexibility might be someone else's jam, I guess.

Things We Like

The fact that the game focuses on scoring more than biffo, especially with models being vastly more resilient than you might expect for a war game, means that Warcrow avoids the common Negative Play Experience of a devastating alpha-strike; you're rarely going to be completely locked out of a game because your opponent got to roll Attack Dice first.

The use of Corruption and Fatigue as resources/risks that can be stretched to breaking point is an excellent way of representing incremental degradation of a fighting force without removing models from the table with a dustpan and brush. It helps keep the game tense and dramatic. It also means that your named special character, Marhael the Refused, hasn't been murked sixteen times over the course of your local campaign. He's not dead, he's just Le Tired.

The sculpts are, as expected from Corvus Belli, amazing. It's an absolute delight to see these models on the battlefield. The advantage to playing a skirmish game is that with such  a low model count, you're not likely to have too many duplicate sculpts on the table at any one time so your army is a gorgeous thing to behold.

The use of the dice system to track not just offence and defence but also trigger status effects and positional play makes the game incredibly enjoyable. You're not just taking turns hitting each other with pointy sticks effectively just trading hit points but each contested roll could see you jockeying for position, blinding your enemy, reducing their morale, loading their mages up with a lethal dose of magical Kool-Aid, all that jazz. It's not enough to count HP, you also have to consider whether you can push an opponent off an objective to stop them scoring or if they can do the same to you. It's a vastly more rewarding game experience than just exchanging punches to see who runs out of living models first.

Things We'd Like to See in the Future

Going to be honest here, the unique movement and distance measurement system of Strides (1 Stride = 2.5 centimetres, so not even an inch) was not a successful experiment. While it's great to build a series of unique value propositions for your game (you need to have a good reason for people to choose to play you game instead of another one, particularly where the industry is dominated by a few well-established properties, cough cough), you also need your game to be accessible and easily understood by your migrating players. Just let people use their measuring tapes. It's such a small quality of life change that I think would help people translate across to this lovely game.

As a minor gripe, while the material they are using for line troops holds detail perfectly well, it does seem to be a more rubbery resin/plastic (plesin?) than whatever they're using for the character units. However, if this material is what's keeping the game's cost of entry down I suppose that's a concession we'll have to make.

Final Thoughts

If you've played Infinity and really enjoyed the quality of sculpts, skirmish-scale and dynamic gameplay but thought to yourself: "Hey, I want this but in a Fantasy setting." then I'd describe Warcrow as about 90% of what you want. Warcrow is a great alternative game to the larger-scale systems in the fantasy space, it's dynamic and keeps both players involved at all times, the models are gorgeous and being a skirmish game you can buy-in relatively cheaply compared to the alternatives. It's not a perfect game and I'd be very interested to see what CB does with the rules in the inevitable 2nd Edition release to help reduce friction but overall it's definitely a winner for me.

Next time we'll talk about some factions, showcase some of the lovely models CB has kindly shared with us, and give you some tips on how to kick off your Warcrow experience.

*Note: The quote referenced here: Reports of my death are greatly exaggerated is, in fact, an exaggeration itself. Today we learned something (Well, I did at least.).

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

A novel Votann combo takes the second undefeated slot here, combining melee brutality from Beserks with one big Hearthguard brick. That combination creates one of the most vicious Rapid Ingress menus out there, and the speed at which this list can carve through foes that disrespect it is staggering. It also makes the interesting choice to run without forts, which reduces the threat projection of the big Beserk squads a bit, but makes the list much more adaptable to terrain, and allows it to fully leverage Hidden. It feels like a far more valid option to exclude them in 11th compared to 10th. The list is rounded off with a fairly high number of small utility pieces, ensuring that it can reliably push buttons for Priority Assets. That Disposition feels very strong with this setup, probably better than either Purge or Recon (the other easily accessible options for Delve), so another great reason to try this combo. T13 on a big hull is now a much more impactful breakpoint when the anti-tank you're worrying about is S12 Hunter profiles rather than S8-10 stuff with Wound modifiers and re-rolls. You just gotta hope and pray you don't run into an Eldar player still defiantly running Fuegan with 10 Fire Dragons. Alongside the big guy you've got a bunch of Cerastus Knights here, and it's worth highlighting that the combination of the magna lascannons and double Atrapos makes this unusually solid at taking down spammed 4W Terminators, also obviously a good place to be right now. Archetype

Trade-focused Aspect Host

Thoughts

Aspect Host tops the 4-1 bracket, going for a classic multi-Phoenix setup supported by Yriel as an additional, reliable trade piece, and various small fast units to support the core, helping the army lock in Recon scoring when required. Extremely fragile, but boy is the damage potential here through the roof, and honestly of spins on Aspect Host I've seen recently, this looks most attractive. Also worth saying that Rhys' only loss was an "only in 11th Edition" 100VP-98VP game against Marcus' Scars. Well done Rhys.

The Best of the Rest

There were 11 more players on 4-1 records. They were:

  • 5th - Sam Young - Adepta Sororitas (Chorus of Condemnation/Bringers of Flame) - Priority Assets: hull spam with double Exorcist.
  • 6th - Bryan Freeman - World Eaters (Vessels of Wrath/Berzerker Warband) - Purge the Foe: Vessels/Warband with double Forgefiend and only a single Berzerker unit.
  • 7th - Dylan Cowan - Dark Angels (Assault Brethren/Darkflight Pursuit/Stormlance Task Force) - Reconnaissance: Ravenwing with bonus melee threats and an Eradipulsor.
  • 8th - Dean Sinnbeck - World Eaters (Butchers of Khorne/Berzerker Warband) - Take and Hold:  30 Terminators, three Helbrutes and Angron, maximum fury.
  • 9th - Matthew Thomas - T'au Empire (Retaliation Cadre) - Purge the Foe: Crisis and Riptides galore.
  • 10th - Ryan Jones - Adeptus Mechanicus (Cohort Cybernetica/Eradication Cohort) - Take and Hold: Cohort² with both Cawl and Thulia plus some Fusiliers for an anti-tank spike.
  • 11th - Erwin Jackson - Aeldari (Fateful Performance/Spirit Conclave) - Disruption: Many Wraiths, the Avatar, and a Troupe in a Starweaver to help with scoring.
  • 12th - Nic Burrows - Iron Hands (Medusa's Wrath/Devastator Brethren) - Purge the Foe: A vicious array of shooty hulls, including Eradipulsors, RepExes, a Redeemer and Brutalis Dreadnoughts, with Feirros overseeing.
  • 13th - Sam Fagan - Space Wolves (Assault Brethren/Saga of the Beastslayer/Stormlance Task Force) - Purge the Foe: Rocket-powered turbo Wulfen, Wolf Scouts with a Sword Phobos Captain (a nasty and unique setup), and Eradipuslors.
  • 14th - Simon Lesa - Orks (Wreckas/Blitz Brigade/Bully Boyz) - Priority Assets: Meganobz with Naz, herohammer, and a Gizmo Battlewagon.
  • 15th - Ryan Toddie - Chaos Knights (Hunting Warpack/Houndpack Lance) - Reconnaissance: Whoops all War Dogs.

Thoughts

The second undefeated slot here went to the Blood Angels, with Jordan unleashing a very nasty high-pressure build. Archetype

Big Infractor

Thoughts

A new take on Emperor's Children to complete our second top four, taking advantage of the bump to base S5 on Infractors. Combining the Frenzied Host and Court buffs, this means a charging unit that's operating alone can be swinging at S6 AP-2 with Sustained Hits and wound re-rolls against a foe on an objective (or anywhere, if they're a Character). As the list title implies, this is very good for carving up 4W Terminators, who are one of the key pillars of the metagame, and will obviously eviscerate anythin less tough than that. The two Detachments also hand out some good defensive tools for the big units. The rest of the list is a mix of classic Emperor's Children pieces, ready to step in and handle whatever targets present themselves. This is a genuine curveball compared to the EC standard, and I'm amused that, as ever, Chaos Marines always seem to come back to the question of "what's the nastiest thing we can put in a Rhino?". We may have a new challenger on that front! Well done Adam!

Wrath makes the army extra durable, and I'm also a fan of the Ancient Weapons bike Captain, since S10 compared to S8 is a much more important breakpoint in a new Marine world. I really like this as a demonstration of solid Dark Angels fundamentals, congratulations Keegan.

Thoughts

Big Bugs vs. Big Boyz here - are there enough Boyz to overcome triple Norn in a take and hold mirror?

It definitely seems plausible that there could be. The bugs have decent damage output, but not really the right tools for killing lots of Boyz fast, unless they roll hot on the Norn blast gun. They will also need to commit two Norns to the central objective to reliably hold onto it, and the Orks really only need to take down one of those for things to start tilting in their direction. With access to Ghaz and a full Flash Gitz unit, I'd expect that to happen and the Orks to take it. However, there are a couple of curveballs that could upend this. Both a good Shadow drop on the Tyranids turn, or the Orks flubbing their roll on a well-timed Savage Roar in theirs, could completely change the game here, as in both those cases it's a while before the Warbosses can remove the shock from their units. Given the bafflingly low scores here on a mission where I'd expect at least a middling floor, my guess is that something like that happpened and it was so catastrophic that the game got called for the Tyranids rather than playing on.

The Best of the Rest

  • 2nd - Jeriah Montano - Orks (Wreckas/Green Tide/Kult of Speed) - Take and Hold: Big Boyz units, a big Gitz squad and some herohammer pieces.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Flyblown Host (Updated August 17, 2026)
content:
In our Detachment Focus series we take a deep dive into an army’s Detachments, covering what’s in them, how they play, and how they’ll fit into the broader meta and your games. In this Detachment Focus we’re looking at the Flyblown Host from the Death Guard.

Originally introduced in the Grotmas 2024 update, the Flyblown Host Detachment received a major overhaul with the release of 11th edition, dropping down to 1 DP and gaining a series of new tricks. This Detachment focuses primarily on your Plague Marines units, giving them some movement tricks and upgrades that can boost their output.

Changelog

  • 10-23-2026 (Current): Updated for post-Q3 Dataslate changes
  • 8-17-2026: Updated for the 11th edition changes
  • 6-25-2025: Updated to reflect FAQ changes
  • 4-26-2025: Updated for the 10th edition Codex
  • 12-1-2024: Initial Publication

Detachment Cost: 1 DP

Force Disposition: Reconnaissance

Unique Tag: FLYBLOWN

The Flyblown Host Detachment focuses purely on buffing Plague Marines, and as a result, its power and utility will largely fluctuate with the power and utility of that unit. The rule here generally lets you give Infiltrators to a number of your units, which can be a solid boon if you're trying to deal with a unit which otherwise struggles to move up the table without a transport. The enhancements here are a solid help as well, with two upgrades for your Plague Marine units on offer. As a Reconnaissance Detachment, this one can push you in some weird directions, but you'll likely be taking a different Disposition from your other Detachment to offset that.

Detachment Rule: Verminous Haze

In the Declare Battle Formations step, you can pick up to two friendly PLAGUE MARINES units to gain Infiltrators.

This is a solid ability to drop on a unit of durable infantry with a 5" move. It helps you position forward and take objectives early while setting up for aggressive turn 1 moves if you're up against an opponent unlikely to punish you for said moves. Of course the big downside to this is that the current layouts often make Infiltrating a massive risk - finding safe spots can be really tricky and if you go second you’re likely to lose your Plague Marines before they can do anything for you. Playing aggressively will often cost you, especially if you end up going second. It can be very tempting to be aggressive with your Plague Marines units, but if you play it too aggressive you’ll just be throwing their points away. That said, if you do have a good spot to drop them, then finding good spots or getting of first turn charges can be a huge deal.

Note that you pick these units long after you’ve picked and attached Leaders, so you can pick a unit with a Leader/Support character to gain Infiltrators.

Credit: Gerald Miller

Enhancements

Both of these are upgrades for Plague Marine units.

  • Insectile Murmuration (Upgrade, 15 points). Goes on a unit of Plague Marines. When the unit targets a unit within Contagion range of a friendly unit, those attacks re-roll wound rolls of 1. This is just very good, as it essentially gives you re-rolls of 1 to wound all the time in melee. 15 Points can be a bit much but if you take this you want this on a big unit of Plague Marines, supported by a pair of characters.
  • Plagueveil (Upgrade, 15 points). Goes on a unit of Plague Marines. Gives them -3” Detection Range. This is cute, but a lot less useful. If you’re taking this Detachment, your Plague Marines are going to be infiltrating forward, in your opponent’s face. This has its best value on a unit in your backfield, holding a home objective, but you don’t use Plague Marines for that, you use Poxwalkers. There's some synergy with your ability to Infiltrate; if you put your Plague Marines behind heavy cover in a forward position this can drop you to a 9" Detection range and help you stay protected even if you've deployed aggressively. That said, you still need to watch out for transports and vehicles which can just close the gap and shoot you in the face.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Stratagems

  • Nauseating Paroxysms (1 CP). Used at the start of the Fight phase on an Engaged Plague Marines unit. Pick a unit they’re engaged with and the enemy has to make a battle-shock roll, with -1 to the roll. This is better than it looks, in part because Plague Marines can take an Icon of Despair, which gives enemy units within 6” -1 to their Leadership. This means they’ll be taking tests at -2 when you use this, and those odds are much, much better. Can be a good way to turn off your opponents’ ability to use Stratagems. That said, this will require you to take an icon, which isn’t the ideal loadout - though it's better now that bolters give you S5, AP-1 shooting. It feels a lot better to take one, anyways. Theoretically this feels geared towards a world where you're using Scabrous Soulrot to give an enemy unit in Contagion Range -1 Leadership as well but at that point you're giving up the faction's best ability (-1 to enemy saves) for a shot at battle-shocking one unit. Just don't.
  • Droning Horror (1 CP). Used in the Shooting phase, when a Plague Marines unit shoots. That unit can re-roll hit rolls of 1, and if their target is within half range, they can re-roll wound rolls of 1. This is a solid little upgrade, and can be nice when you’re fishing for 5+ crits with meltaguns, plasma guns, and blight launchers on a unit with a Biologus Putrifier. That said, it isn’t that big a boost, and Plague Marine shooting (especially the shooting that rolls to hit) isn’t great, so this isn’t something you’re going to use often, in part because you often take plague spewers/sprayers with Plague Marines, and you can get re-rolls to wound with the Enhancement.
  • Eye of the Swarm (1 CP). Used in your Shooting phase when a friendly Plague Marines unit shoots. That unit’s ranged attacks have [CLOSE QUARTERS]. This on the other hand, is straight fire, and great for just shooting your way out of combat when your turn comes around. You may not be able to fall back and shoot/charge, but just killing the unit in combat with you is a fine consolation. Fire it off and push through your enemy into the next unit.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Playing This Detachment

Remember when we said the value of this Detachment fluctuates with the strength of Plague Marines? Well, Plague Marines aren't particularly great right now. They managed to dodge some point hikes in the latest balance update thanks to already being T6, and their bolters are better, but you're still not taking bolters if you can avoid it and being able to Infiltrate isn't as good as it sounds when it can often mean getting blown off the board on the first turn.

The other challenge here is Reconnaissance. It's not really a Disposition Death Guard and Plague Marine-heavy armies want to play with, so you'll want to pick up an alternative with your second Detachment. There your options are:

  • Shamblerot Vectorium - This does nothing for you, and Disruption is a worse disposition. If you're running Shamblerot, run Paragons with it instead.
  • Tallyband Summoners - This one is more focused on the idea of taking a lot of big, nasty threats (Rotigus, Mortarion, Great Unclean One), with Plague Marine bricks to support them as surprisingly fast units to spread contagion with an extra 3" to their range. Like Shamblerot, only adds Disruption, making it more of a teams pick.
  • Mortarion's Hammer - This one's going to focus more on putting your Plague Marines in a land raider or another transport, then driving said transport through a wall. Big advantage here is getting Purge the Foe as your Disposition.
  • Champions of Contagion - The best secondary option, this one actually focuses on the characters who will be attaching to your Plague Marines. Gives you Take and Hold.

If you're running this Detachment, it'll likely be with Champions of Contagion, which will let you switch contagions mid-game for your army. That can be cute if you're using something like Nauseating Paroxysms to cause battle-shock tests and mess with enemy leadership but the reality is that you just want -1 to saves (Rattlejoint Ague) most if not all of the time. After all, dead units can't pass Leadership tests. The real gems in this Detachment for you are the Malignance Magnified (re-roll hits and wounds against a unit below starting strength), and Grotesque Fortitude (+2 Toughness for a phase), both of which help you get more out of your 10-model Plague Marine units.

Strengths

  • Plague Marines. This Detachment does a crazy good job buffing Plague Marines, and Infiltrating them can be very scary.
  • Eye of the Swarm. Shooting your way out of combat is huge, and helps solve a key problem for Plague Marines.

Weaknesses

  • Plague Marines. Plague Marines aren't great right now - a little too expensive, a little too weak in the output department. This Detachment is only as good as they are useful at any given moment.

Final Thoughts

If you're running Death Guard and want to take big bricks of Plague Marines, this is the Detachment for you. You're likely going to pair it with Champions of Contagion, as that both encourages you to take characters who attach to Plague Marines and also gives you more options to play with on the table.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews Warhammer The Old World: Arcane Journal River of Bones
content:
Falcon: As 2026 comes to an end, James Workshop has blessed us Old World players with our final Arcane Journal of the year, and at first glance it is a bit of a mixed bag. River of Bones has a surprising amount of content, with roughly 25 pages of lore and 20 pages of rules including two and a half new Armies of Infamy, the return of Mysterious terrain from previous editions (now called Enchanted), new cursed core magic items, and more Wood Elf kindreds. Yet, other than a couple of highlights it feels like this book might be the dreaded reverse Sum41: All Filler No Killer. That is a deep cut just for you Canadian millennials out there. Who knows though, just like my opinion on Sum41, I’ve been wrong before; so let’s dive into it and y’all can be the judge.

An Enchanting Addition

Previous editions of Warhammer Fantasy Battle prominently featured mystery terrain features, where forests, rivers, and ruins would alter the state of the game once the first model toed into their borders. Trees could be filled with snakes or awaken and slap unfortunate souls that chose to move too quickly through them. Rivers could enrage or heal the models that waded into their depths. Ruins could be haunted or cast random spells. For players that loved the anarchy, the narrative, or the layer of challenge they added to the game they were well-enjoyed, while others hated how they could tip the scales because they hated fun. Well, now all of that is back with the Enchanted terrain rule. This optional rule for your games causes all natural terrain features on the board to potentially have an additional effect that is rolled for when the first model enters the terrain piece. Unlike previous editions where there were separate tables for the different terrain types you could expect, enchanted terrain utilizes a singular 2d6 table for all of them and has effects that range from permanent reductions to movement speed, to ward saves, to abject violence being meted out on the poor souls looking for a place to hide. If you’re looking to occasionally add an extra layer of spice to your games this is a welcome little tweak that I highly recommend.

Why Are We Here?

Liam: The story is great here; Settra is rampaging north and it out just to really show the forces of the Bretonnian who's actually boss, continuing the story from previous books. He rampages through Renegade Princes and fends off an army of Dwarfs without breaking sweat. While some of his lieutenants may not always fair so well Settra is very much untroubled by any of it and marches to the foot of Louen Keep ready to enforce his will. What is also great is that at one point he sends off a High Priest to investigate some Tombs, as you do, but the High Priest ends up coming out the other side and finds the boarder of Athel Loren, he doesn't want to enter, but it's just too tempting, he can't help himself so in he goes, against his better judgement.

There's loads of additional background material on the forces of the Nehekhara filling us in on how they want to collect knowledge and despite their leaders massive lifespans haven't remotely began to quench that first. I'm not usually a big "reading" guy for the most part but I'm enjoyed reading this and it's certainly fed into the cannon inside of head for how these armies work and grow over time.

We then head back to the forces of Ashurtak and their foray into Athel Loren. I'm not going to go into lots of details here because it's for you to enjoy but I wondered why the book was called "The River of Blood," and after reading this I'm no longer left asking this question.

On Barrowed Time

Peter: Next up in this tome, we find essentially two Armies of Infamy for the Tomb Kings related to the Barrow Kings. The first of which, the Champions of Nehekhara, is Battle Marches exclusive, which is very interesting as it opens up more options for people trying to play with the limited points in that format. One of the problems with the Battle March format for grand army Tomb Kings players, is their need for a Hierophant as well as a general and how that shoehorns your lists in order to make it remotely possible. This list follows all of the normal Grand Army composition requirements for the Tomb Kings but removes the option of taking actual Tomb Kings and High Priests along with their 1+ needs, instead letting you lead your army with a Royal Herald or Necrotect should you desire

(though you may still choose to take a Prince or Mortuary Priest).

In addition to this, Royal Heralds in a Champions of Nehekhara battle march army gain the Honour Thy King special rule. This rule grants any unit joined by a Royal Herald either a +1 to their movement speed, reroll hit rolls of 1 in the combat phase, or +D3 to their initiative. It should be noted that this rule cannot affect a unit also affected by My Will Be Done.

Finally, if you elect to run a Champions of Nehekhara list in your Battle March games and have a Royal Herald or Tomb Prince as your general with no Mortuary Priest to back them up, your general gains the Arch Hierophant special rule, allowing them to attempt to resurrect infantry or cavalry units in your command phase though they are much worse at doing it than their clerics.

All that said, if Battle Marches are not your jam, the Barrow Kingdoms Army of Infamy is here to quench your unending thirst for subjugating the sands. This AoI, representing the disparate Barrow Kingdoms that exist near the Skull mountains, requires you to take 1+ Tomb Prince or Royal Herald rather than a Tomb King, as well has 1+ High Priest or Mortuary priest. Note that should you use that 1+ on a High Priest, you cannot take any further, as they are both a 1+ and 0-1 in this list which could be confusing on first read through. It would also lock you out from bringing a Tomb King, so you must choose wisely when building out your characters in this AoI.

In core, you are required to take 1+ units of Skeleton Archers or Warriors, as well as however many Skeleton Skirmishers, Horsemen, Horse Archers or Chariots you desire, and up to 1 unit of Tomb Guard. The big units you’ll be missing out on if you choose this army over the others are in Special and Rare as Ushabti and the Casket of Souls (and Carrion if

you’re into that kind of thing) disappear, replaced with the Winged Warsphinx from the last TK aligned Arcane Journal.

As far as special rules go, the Barrow Kingdoms have 5, though 3 are simply GW’s new way of creating specialist units for a faction without building out an entirely new datasheet for an existing unit with 1 or 2 extra rules. Battle Wizards is the first rule here, and the main reason to consider running this army composition over any of the others. In addition to their normal Lores of Magic, Liche Priests of the Barrow Kingdoms may know spells from the lores of Battle and Dark. If you’re looking to run a more aggressive Tom Guard list in a post-1.5.3 world, this is probably where you’re going to do it. Getting access to Frenzy and Hatred from Dark magic or Arcane Urgency/Oaken Shield on your big brick or Sphinxes on top of the benefits given by a Necrotect can make for a scary elite unit that can protect your mid-table and project a threat that is hard to avoid.

Finest Charioteers and Noble Cavalry are next. The first of these rules allow you to upgrade 0-2 of your Skeleton Chariot units for +6 points per model, giving them +1 initiative, First Charge, Khopesh and most importantly a 5+ regeneration save. Given how cheap Chariots have become in recent FAQs, this is a pretty spicy upgrade to have in your back pocket and opens up some pretty devastating flank potential. The cavalry upgrade grants 0-2 of your Skeleton Horsemen units regeneration 5+, a weapon skill of 3 and the Khopesh special rule for 3ppm. Liam: In my head these are both great upgrades, especially the chariots. I'm a big fan of this way of "boosting" units to give new options rather than just making a new version of similar things. I know these are top tier upgrades but they're good upgrades and something I'm looking forward to seeing on the table.

Skeleton Skirmishers also see a cool upgrade in this AoI. For +3ppm, 0-2 units may be

upgraded to Shades of Death, making them Ethereal and giving their bows the Magical Attacks special rule. Liam: It goes without saying just how ridiculously game breaking this upgrade could be. Magic Weapons are limited to a handful of models in most armies and while Magic Missiles exist they're still not easily going to kill 20 models with a 6+ regeneration save. I haven't had real chance to put this on the table yet but I'm fairly sure that nearly every time I write a list for this ends up with me putting in 1x20, if not 2x20 Skeleton Skirmishers just to pose opponents problems.

Falcon: The final special rule for the Barrow Kingdoms, Vassals of the Great Land, gives all Royal Heralds in a Barrow Kingdoms list the Honour thy King special rule we spoke about in the Battle March army of infamy on top of allowing your army general the option to ride a Necrolith Bone Dragon as a mount even if they normally would not be allowed to.

All-in-all, from a purely competitive perspective I do not think this pushes out the Royal Host or Grand Army in terms of power as of the writing of this article, but there are some really interesting things here to set you apart. Access to Dark and Battle Magic are big deals though they are hampered a bit by the restrictions on High Priests in the army.

The Woods Are Lovely, Dark and Deep

While the Tomb Kings side of this journal feels a bit lackluster, particularly given the range

refresh being released along with these rules, Wood Elf players have a few more things to be excited about with two new and improved monsters, a truly dedicated forest spirit Army of Infamy, and most importantly for those of you looking to make the most of your lists in grindier games, new kindreds.

The Spirits of the Forest Army of Infamy is up first, and while it lacks the bevy of special rules other Armies of Infamy have had, it still manages to create a brand new way to play your models through a unique army composition list. In terms of what you are allowed to bring, your character choices are locked to 0-1 Ancient or Gargantuan Ancient Treeman per 1000 points, 0-1 Spellweavers, and any number of Glade Captains, Spellsingers or Branchwraiths. No Shadowdancers, Dragonlords, or Wayfinders make their way into these lists.

At Core, Dryads are a mandatory piece at 1+ units per army with Glade Guard and Deepwood Scouts listed at 1 per 1000pts. The big piece here for players is that a single unit of Treekin, sporting their fresh new Toughness 6 duds, can be slotted into your core so long as your general is a Treeman of some kind.

The Special slot sees Deepwood Scouts, Eternal Guard, more Glade Guard, Wardancers,

Wildwood Rangers, Tree Kin, Glade Riders and Sisters of the Thorn as option, while Rare (at a heaping 33% of your list if you want it) is taken up by the old Treeman or 0-1 Gargantuan Treemen per 1000 points.

This list does have some serious potential, though it runs pretty slow with no kitted Glade Lords to project combat threat. That said, having access to a T6 unit in your core slot and the potential of running 4 Toughness 6+ monsters (we’ll get to those shortly) leads to some unique opportunities for a faction normally reliant on evasiveness, and could be a real winner in team play in particular.

For special rules, the Spirits of the Forest have just two. Deepwood Ambush is the first and is relatively simple. Dryads and Treekin may have the Ambushers special rule for +1 point per model and Branchwraiths and all varieties of Treeman may have it for +10 points. Additionally, any unit coming in from ambush may choose to enter play completely within the boundaries of a forest so long as they are not within 6 inches of an enemy model. I’m not gonna lie, this is a flavorful and sassy ability if only situationally useful. Unlike the Green Knight that just needs an inch of space to pop up and choose violence, 6 inches is a pretty big gap to maintain and can be easily countered with positional play. That said, it is another thing opponents will need to think about whenever you toss a unit into ambush and there is a world where ambushing a chunk (or all of if you are an absolute madman) of your army will save you points regardless of the fickleness of the ability. Liam: There is a big difference between fitting in a single base and an entire unit of Dryads or a Treeman.

Falcon: The second rule is Blessings of the Elder Wood. This rule grants access to a unique set of what are essentially magic items with their own allotment, just for Forest Spirit characters in this Army of Infamy. Any Forest Spirit character in this army of infamy may select 1 of the blessings, though the new Gargantuan Treeman and it’s Ancient Gargantuan kin may take 1 regardless of the army they’re found in. They are:

Blessings of the Oak. This 50 point blessing is pretty stellar, granting the bearer Armoured Hide (1) and immunity to Killing Blow, Monster Slayer, and Multiple Wounds (X), instead suffering just a single wound if hit with any of those abilities. Bumping your Treemen up to a 3+ Save AND granting them this kind of protection will keep them up and moving for way longer than they have any right to and I would expect to see this upgrade in every Forest Spirit list from now until eternity.

Blessings of the Ash. At 45 points, this is the other big boy blessing to be had in the list,

granting it’s bearer a +1 to their regeneration saves (getting those Treemen to a very respectable 4+) AND forcing enemy models to reroll any natural to hit rolls of 6 both in combat and at range.

Blessings of the Willow. For 40 points, this upgrade grants its bearer Magic Resistance (-2) and provides them with a 5+ Ward save against Magical Attacks.

Blessings of the Yew. Finally, the Yew Tree is a 30 point blessing that allows its bearer to stand back up after losing its last wound on a roll of a 2+. On a 2-5 the bearer will have 1 wound remaining, on a 6 they will gain D3. This one is pretty lacklustre, I generally dislike when rules like this have an additional failure point when you are paying additional points for them.

Liam: This is really weird because these are all good, and if you could buy them for your monster/character in a lot of armies you'd nearly always pick one up, even the Blessing of the Yew while not amazing means you can be a little bit more reckless with your characters. But the problem here is that the Blessing of the Oak is ridiculously good. I mean it's so far ahead of the rest that it might as well cost 80pts and only be available on the Character version. I'm not totally sold we'll see loads of these on the table but what I can be sure of is that if we do they'll nearly all be Blessed by the Oak.

Last March of the Ents

The Gargantuan Treeman and Gargantuan Treeman Ancient are the new additions to the Wood Elf arsenal and may be taken in the Spirits of the Forest AoI as listed above or as a 0-1 Character option for the Ancient and 0-1 Rare option for the plain jane gargantuan model in the Wood Elf Realms Grand Army.

As far as Behemoths go, these fellas are a bit beefier than their smaller cousins coming in at Strength 6, Toughness 7, and with 7 wounds compared to the normal Treeman and Ancient’s 6 Toughness and 5 wounds. The Gargantuan Treeman also boasts 6 attacks at Weapon Skill 6 and is a lvl 1 wizard with access to Battle Magic, Elementalism, and the Lore of the Wilds. The Ancient Gargantuan sacrifices 2 Weapon Skill and 2 Attacks in exchange for being a lvl 2 Wizard and having access to 100 points of Forest Spites compared the Gargantuan Treeman’s 50. On top of all of this, both new Treemen get bumped to D6 Stomp attacks and trade the old Strangleroot attack for a MUCH more impressive 24 inch Str 3 AP -1 (Str 6, Multiple Wounds D3+1 in the centre) Stone Thrower attack using the 5 inch template with the Move and Shoot special rule. Lastly, these Treemen are on 100x150 bases which indicates they are to be played with their Age of Sigmar (8th Ed WHFB) models or perhaps a new model coming down the line, given just how small the original Treeman would look on that absurd base.

The only real problem with these guys is the price tag. At 300 base points for the Gargantuan Treeman, 325 for the Ancient and the effectively mandatory 45-50 point upgrades to help ensure their survival against the seemingly infinite cannons, ogre blades, and wrecked flails that permeate the Old World, it can be difficult to find space for these brutes in a meta that values higher movement speed, swiftstride, and core units that can play the objective game. Also, the loss of attacks and weapon skill is an insane drop in value to be paying 25 points extra and only getting 1 lvl of wizardry in return.

Dreaded Kindreds

When the Wood Elf Arcane Journal was released, one of the high-points was the incredibly

powerful list of kindred upgrades for your elven characters and the same is true of this release as Wood Elf players gain access to a further 6 to elevate your lists. Unlike the previous release, these ‘kinbands’ are actually for your units of Glade Guard, Glade Riders, Eternal Guard, Wildwood Rangers, and Deepwood Scouts rather than the characters and a few are flat out fire.

Note that these kinbands are 1 per unit but are repeatable throughout your list and only one of them applies any further restrictions on your army.

Kinbands of Cavaroc (+15pts per Unit): Grants the unit +1 to the movement and the

Vanguard Special rule. Not a terrible upgrade, but there are better ones for sure.

Kinbands of Argwylon (+10pts per Unit): Grants the unit Magic Resistance (-1). Very cheap access to MR (-1) is nice if you have the points.

Kinbands of Athylwyth (+2pts per Model): Units with this upgrade Reroll To-Hit rolls of 1 in shooting and combat, you cannot have more than 1 unit with the Tree Spirit rule in your list per 1000 points. Rerolls are hard to come by in this edition and this penalty is a very minor one as most Grand Army lists are only running 1-2 units of Tree Spirits anyway.

Kinbands of Modryn (+2pts per Model): Units with this upgrade Reroll To-Wound rolls of 1 during the Shooting Phase. This upgrade being locked to the shooting phase is really its only weakness and is a strong selection if you’re going all in on say a unit of Glade Guard, though there is probably one better.

Kinbands of Cythral (+1pt per Model): Models with this upgrade automatically pass

dangerous terrain tests and receive a 5+ ward save against any unit with the troop type

Monster. This is an excellent upgrade for the units of Wildwood Rangers we sometimes see

tossed into competitive lists as it greatly upgrades their survivability when doing the thing they do best.

Kinbands of Torgovann (+1pt per Model): The greatest of the kinbands and it is not even close in my opinion. Models in a unit with this upgrade select a non-magical weapon they are equipped, that weapon has its armour piercing characteristic improved by 1. Asrai longbows are already decent threats in a wood elf list, giving them an additional pip of AP is a huge upgrade for a single point. I feel we’ll be seeing this tossed on a number of units with abandon.

Barrow Relics

The last bit of love in this journal are the new core magic items made available to every non-dwarven faction in the times before. Like the last Arcane Journal, these items are cursed, and so they all come with some kind of negative effect that theoretically brings down their overall cost. Unlike the last Arcane Journal, there aren't really as many bangers as were to be found in the March of Chaos.

Liam: It's worth noting that these are new Common magic items and can be taken by anyone. I'm all in on new random magic items in books when they've thought of ones they'd like to add to the game.

Falcon: Still, there are a couple of situationally sweet treats for the right connoisseurs. Of the 18 items available, here are the standouts:

The Briar Bow. For 25 points, this Range 30, Str 3, AP -1 bow has some real potential in the right hands. When this bow successfully strikes an enemy unit, roll an artillery die to determine how many hits the unit actually takes. On a misfire result, the bearer of the bow is hit once instead and the bow is destroyed. The potential upside here is quite powerful, with each bowshot having the potential to really neuter enemy units and the downside is well priced as a single str 3 hit is relatively easy to survive under most circumstances.

The Armour of Fate. At 35 points, this piece of Heavy Armour has a lot of potential in the right list. Infantry or Cavalry Only. Bearers of this armour reroll all failed armour save rolls (suck it dawnstone), if the reroll result is a natural 1, they take a strength 5 hit with no armour save permitted. Any build that can reliably get down to a 2 or 3+ armour save is going to love adding this piece to their repetoire, as any WHFB player that ever got stuck in with a Saurus Cowboy in the age of 8th edition will be sure to testify.

Robes of Phakth. This 50 point enchanted item seems a bit pricy at first especially as it is infantry only, but it grants the bearer the Ethereal, Fly(8) and Loner special rules. There are a number of dedicated combat characters out there that become extremely difficult to deal with with the extra layer of protection Ethereal provides and there is just enough room here for a Flail of Wrecks and Charmed Shield to round out the build in basically every army that wants it.

The Tome of Oppression. This item actually isn't particularly good outside of Legacy factions but it is unique and for that it deserves some credit. For 40 points, this arcane item may be used in place of a dispel attempt once per turn. Instead of attempting to beat an enemy's casting result, the bearer and the caster both roll a d6 and add their toughness value. If the bearer's result is greater, the spell is dispelled and the enemy wizard suffers a Str 4 hit with an AP value of -1. If the casting wizard is successful, it is the bearer that takes that hit. Units like Troll Hags, Chaos Dwarf Sorcerers and Slaughtermasters, can get a lot of mileage out of this item.

Final Thoughts

The River of Bones has a lot of content to offer, though much of it is bogged down in middling rules. That said, as I typed out this review I became more enamored with bits that I originally disliked. While I don't necessarily think the Armies of Infamy in this book are particularly strong, there is something here. The kinbands are a strict upgrade to just about every wood elf list, a couple of the magic items will potentially shake up what has been a stale meta, and I'm curious to see if the Gargantuan Treemen will make any kind of waves.

Liam: It's not a bad book, and I think my initial impression of there being very little here has kind of fallen away. I think that they're clearly trying to add a little and often to lots of different factions in Warhammer: The Old World and it's through this that we're going to learn about the world and it's inhabitants. I think we'll see a fair amount of the TK AOI but needs some skill to get right and applying the Ethereal units in the key locations and while the Gargantuan Treemen won't fit every style of Wood Elf list there's certainly something in taking a T6 unit in your core, multiple T6 monsters and a couple of T7 ones and just saying "can you deal with this?" in the same way Knights posed that question in 40k for years. Will everyone be overjoyed by the additions? Unlikely. But I'm excited to try them out.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!
