title: How Trench Crusade tells some of the most exciting stories in miniature wargames
content:
Trench Crusade's unique blend of historic warfare and gruesome Catholic fantasy make it one of the most striking miniature wargames of recent years. Mike Franchina's delightfully nasty art opens the door to a world I'd hate to live in, but I'm desperate to explore. Those initial images are also backed up by some of the most enticing, entrail-laden lore in the modern hobby. What is it that makes it so damned exciting?

For the uninitiated, Trench Crusade takes place on an alternate Earth where Crusaders opened a Hellmouth in Jerusalem. For the next 800 years, demonic forces flooded the world and tried to take it from the faithful and mortal. The wars you know were waged, but this time, humanity fights the forces of Hell. Now, it's 1914, and the battle between Fallen and Faithful takes place in the trenches of No Man's Land.

Longtime wargamer Tim Linward says this is the best grimdark storytelling since early 2000s Games Workshop. Personally, I'm much newer to the world of wargames - but Trench Crusade compels me just the same. I find myself drawn to its gruesome sanctity, its gnarly monstrosities, and its portrayal of humanity - both horrid and holy.

That's why I jumped at the chance to chat with former Mordheim designer Tuomas Pirinen about Trench Crusade's deep, dark lore. Wargamer has asked Pirinen for all sorts of wisdom, from slick rules design to mentoring the next generation of wargame designers. Now, I have a new question: if God is real, what is Trench Crusade trying to tell him?

Pirinen's answer is personal rather than explicitly canon. He's written basically the entire timeline of Trench Crusade, and all the gory details in-between, but faith is a personal thing - even when it's in a fictional world.

"I believe that, in order for there to be free will, God can't just solve your problems", he tells me. "In the Trench Crusade universe, we are God's children, and you've got to let your children grow up and make their own mistakes. This war was started by humans opening the gates of Hell, by their own free will."

God, then, takes a hands-off approach in Trench Crusade. Even when the word of God powers Faithful troops, humanity has engineered it. Strange mutations and arcane machines fuel their forces, though the cost of that firepower is desecrating the temples we call mind and body. Pirinen tells me this is well within tradition for stories inspired by Christianity.

"Tolkien was extremely clear that The Lord of the Rings is a Christian, Catholic book", he says, "and yet God doesn't interfere". "Eru Ilúvatar, Tolkien's version of the Catholic God, isn't throwing thunderbolts or resurrecting people. But when Gollum betrayed Frodo at Mount Doom, he slipped, not because God pushed him, but because God built a world where a betrayal born from free will suffers the consequences."

Tolkien himself fought in World War One, though his whereabouts in the Trench Crusade canon remains unknown. It'll probably stay that way, too. While many real world figures feature, from Jean d'Arc to Catherine of Sienna, Pirinen doesn't want to simply repeat history.

"One of the most common questions we get is 'what about Napoleon?' 'What about the Red Baron?' 'What about Tolkien?' But if you do all that, it gets very gimmicky." "Plus, you need to do a lot of research, because we want to do justice to any character from real-world history. Then, it starts becoming not your world or your story."

Trench Crusade's roots in reality make it more affecting, Pirinen says, and he thinks that's one of the reasons the wargame has been such a runaway success. "When we show a map of the Trench Crusade world, everybody looks at what's happening at home - and you don't get that with a pure fantasy world", he tells me.

Still, Trench Crusade cherishes its creative freedom. It means the designers can explore the "fascinating history" of countries like Ukraine and Ethiopia, but free of real-world events like war, occupation, and colonialism that strip these nations of agency.

"That's much more interesting than repeating history", Pirinen says. "People who normally don't get featured in wargames get to have agency." "I'm super proud we have players in Turkey and Africa, which isn't common at all for a wargame", he adds, "so I want to explore these areas too."

Alternate histories aside, sometimes the truth is actually stranger than fiction. Take the throwing crosses you can wield as weapons. "We get a lot of people saying 'but this is a complete fantasy!'", Pirinen says "It's real. 100%. They were real weapons."

It's a careful balance of creativity and authenticity, but Trench Crusade nails it to a cross. Both are backed up by huge amounts of care and research. Real Catholic Clerics help craft the lore behind the wargame. Pirinen even interviewed veterans of the Finnish Civil War, so Trench Crusade's mechanics better represent the reality of Trench warfare.

"It isn't a simulation game, but I wanted you to actually feel like you're taking these daring dashes, throwing a grenade, and following up with a bayonet charge", he says. "I wanted the lore, art, miniature, and mechanics to fulfill the fantasy, exactly as imagined."

Dig underneath the interesting details, and you find what truly makes Trench Crusade lore compelling. It's a big question, one that's easy to empathize with: "When you are fighting the literal forces of Hell, how far can you go before you are indistinct from your enemies?"

Trench Crusade is a world where evil is real and tangible, and all humanity has banded together to resist it. But humans are far from righteous do-gooders. They mutilate themselves and others, use doctrine to manipulate, and even throw children into the line of fire. "Even if you're fighting a just war", Pirinen says, "it's easy to go too far."

These are the building blocks of a lore that truly enthralls. A profound premise, elevated by authentic real-world histories backed up by careful research. Throw in some of grimdark's most creative minis, art, and storylines, and you've got a world that, however horrific, I'm dying to enter.

Trench Crusade and its 10/10 Carcass Front box set, are currently available at Essen. I've even more stories to tell straight from the booth, so sign up to the Wargamer Discord to hear them first.

Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

A glorious showdown which highlights some thoughts I had a couple of weeks ago when the changes for Ad Mech first game through. I've not commented on them on  here yet - WHAT THE HELL, balance team. Shoving 5 dps into one list from very competitive and dangerous detachments whilst doing nothing remotely similar for any other faction isn't a good look. Ad Mech were already performing very consistently.

That said, the resulting Eradication builds have been, how do I put this? Greedy. Greedy as hell. All damage, no finesse, and grabbing the Take and Hold disposition. Ad Mech historically aren't the top dogs in this department - many other more brutal pressure type armies prefer that landscape. I have watched new Ad Mech tearing up the competitive world behind the scenes, and it's starting to filter out elsewhere now too. If there is a saving grace, it is probably in the slight weakness as a Take and Hold army Ad Mech have, which is being run down.

Enter the Blood Angels. Historically a really tough match up for Ad Mech because of their speed and ability to simply run through almost every defensive profile they have. This list packs in Dreadnoughts and Sang Guard, as well as forward pressure pieces to skirmish and tag. The combination here is enough to actually cleave through, then tie up the Ad Mech lines. Clustered Ad Mech units are vulnerable to massed overrun connects too. These are the kinds of list I expect to give the new hotness pause, and so it proved here.

Thoughts

I think it's fair to say people have slept a little on Blood Angels. Much of the attention in recent times has been on other special boy chapters, or the eternal Ultramarines. However, I think something is cooking here at the moment. The additional reach of the doctrines is MASSIVE for the army, which is now able to close the gap, tag, and then fall back and cause havoc. The toughness boosts are subtle on this army but do enough that they aren't simply falling over to small arms fire across the board. There is a real overload army here again, and I am loving the lists combining them with the Dreadnoughts at the moment. Sensational work on the event win.

Archetype

Biomasses

Thoughts

A chunky take on the Bio / Xenomasses combo I myself initiated at edition launch. Robin has built on that formula really nicely here, adding in Bio / Primus support to the damage packages to help them genuinely punch through brick units. GSC live and die by getting the damage through, and this version feels far more able to consistently do so in the face of ever tougher bricks. Slightly less enemy units on the board in many match ups benefits GSC - Robin took full advantage here. Well done!

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Paragons of Putrescence
content:
In our Detachment Focus series we take a deep dive into an army’s Detachments, covering what’s in them, how they play, and how they’ll fit into the broader meta and your games. In this Detachment Focus we’re looking at the Contagion Engines Detachment for the Death Guard.

The Death Guard received three new 1 DP Detachments at the onset of 11th edition, each of which catered to a different unit type in the army. Of these, the Paragons of Putrescence focuses on the army's CHARACTER units, and as a result acts as the Detachment with the widest use among those 1 DP options.

Detachment Cost: 1 DP

Force Disposition: Priority Assets

This is a character-focused Detachment, and that means it can pair with a large number of builds and Detachments, but will primarily favor those running Plague Marines or Terminators. Notably, you can pair this one with Champions of Contagion, and that means a bit more when you have both extra Contagion Range and the ability to customize/do more with your Contagion. This is also the ideal paired Detachment for Shamblerot Vectorium, where you want to get more out of your large units of Poxwalkers with attached characters and Mortarion. Giving you the Priority Assets Disposition is an added bonus there, since it stops you from having to play Disruption.

Detachment Rule: Hypervirulent Strains

Friendly DEATH GUARD CHARACTER units have +3” to their Contagion Range (to a max of 12”).

This is just a great buff to have on all the time, and gives you 6” range in the first battle round - that’s a lot to work with, and makes your job tagging units in those early turns way easier. This also works on Mortarion, giving the big guy an extra menacing aura to work with as he floats around the table. If you combine this with Death Lord’s Chosen you can get some silly range on your mortal wounds ability, and it’s solid when you’re doubling upon on Contagions in Death Lord’s Chosen. It's also fine on Poxwalkers led by characters, though you'll lose the ability to Infiltrate when you attach to those units, so the benefits are somewhat limited in that regard. Having 9" contagion range on round 2 can really make some nasty tricks possible, such as daisy chaining deep striking units of Deathshrouds.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Enhancements

  • Rejuvenating Swarm (20 points). Goes on a non-TERMINATOR INFANTRY model only. Attacks targeting this unit with S greater than their T have -1 to wound rolls. This is great for improving the durability of Plague Marines, where being T6 and having -1 to wound from bigger attacks is just a really solid buff on a unit that can be surprisingly fragile. You know where it's even better, though? On a unit of 20 Poxwalkers, where you can make them even more of a pain in the ass to pick up. -1 to wound is even better when it's on T4 models who are more likely to eat 3+ rolls.
  • Host of the Hybridised Pox (40 points). INFANTRY model only. Once per battle, per army, in your Command phase, you can use this ability. If you do, you pick one of the plagues in Nurgle’s Gift and until the end of the battle your unit gets that plague in addition to the one you chose. This is also pretty neat, and a fun way to get -1 to be hit on top of the -1 to saves from Rattlejoint Ague. It’s cute, but probably not worth spending points. That said, you can combine this with Cornucophagus in Champions of Contagion to have all three effects in play at once. For 40 points, this is just a bit too much to spend, and the reality is that the -1 to saves plague is really all you need.

Stratagems

  • Territorial Infection (1 CP). Used at the start of the Command phase on a CHARACTER unit to give that unit +1 OC until the end of the turn. This is a really great way to steal an objective, and particularly useful on Deathshroud Terminators, where a unit going from 4 OC to 8 can make a big difference, but can also be useful for getting Plague Marines up to 3 OC each. It’s a big brain play that can cause a lot of problems if your opponent isn’t ready for it and it can be used in your opponent’s turn. It's also amazing when you can throw it on a blob of 20 Poxwalkers to suddenly hold a crapload of table space and steal both middle objectives.
  • Aggravus Spasms (1 CP). Used at the start of your Shooting phase on a friendly Death Guard CHARACTER unit. Pick one visible enemy unit within Contagion Range of your unit and that unit gets +6” Detection range. This is interesting - it means you can tag a unit within 9” on round 2 and give it 21” Detection Range, but if you’re within 9” you’re already just going to light that unit up and/or charge it. It’s an interesting ability but I’m not sure how much you’ll actually use it. Helpful for those times when Poxwalkers are outkicking your coverage, usually when you're being supported by Defilers and/or a Knight.
  • Simultaneous Contamination (1 CP). Used in your Shooting phase, when a CHARACTER unit starts an Action. The unit can still shoot while it does the action. This is nifty, and handy if your plan is to play Priority Assets or for those rare turns you draw Cleanse or Plunder. Pretty situational otherwise, though. It only lets you shoot, so the value is going to be more around taking extra shots with your Malignant Plaguecasters or units of Plague Marines, or for when Mortarion needs to hang back.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Playing This Detachment

This is just a really versatile Detachment, and your go-to if you're running one of the other 2 DP options, as there's no world where you aren't taking at least a few characters. As we've mentioned, the most competitive way to use this Detachment is alongside Shamblerot Vectorium, where you get access to both Priority Assets - fine for an army running 7+ units of Poxwalkers - and the Rejuvenating Swarm Enhancement, which usually goes on a Noxious Blightbringer attached to a 20-model Poxwalkers unit alongside Typhus to create a nasty blob with extra movement, better healing, and added durability against incoming attacks. This is the current competitive list for Death Guard, and whether you play Priority Assets or Disruption will largely depend on whether you're playing in a Teams event (Teams events favor Disruption as this army does an OK job running it and someone has to jump on that particular grenade).

After that, you can get mileage out of Aggravus Spasms if you're being supported by Defilers or a Knight Despoiler, since it's about debuffing an enemy unit near one of your CHARACTER units - increasing a unit's detection range by 6" is quite a bit, and you can really open up on opponents who otherwise thought they were safe. Simultaneous Contamination is one that has limited utility given Poxwalkers can't shoot, but it's good to have in your back pocket for those times Mortarion wants to do an action and shoot and isn't in charge range of anything.

Strengths

  • Rejuvenating Swarm. This is a crazy good Enhancement and makes big units of Poxwalkers insanely annoying to try and take down.
  • Versatile. Buffing characters with extra contagion range is just always good, and you're always bringing characters.

Weaknesses

  • No real offensive buffs. Extra contagion range is nice but also not necessarily something you need, especially after round 3, and the real buff here is just a defensive buff you pay for on a single unit.

Final Thoughts

If you're running Death Guard competitively, chances are you're taking this one. It pairs wonderfully with Shamblerot Vectorium and the characters you want to take there, and gives you a much better disposition option. The Stratagems here are fine, the abilities solid, and most of your non-vehicle units are either characters or able to have attached characters, making this one that most of your army can use effectively.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Godeater's Son, by Noah van Nguyen
content:
credit: Black Library

With the release of Blood of the Godeater, let’s take a look at the first of Noah Van Nguyen’s books about the Chaos warlord, Heldanarr Fall.

Gentrification has hit Candip, an ancient and proud city in some hot dusty corner of Aqshy. The native tribes of the region, who had weathered the horrors of the Age of Chaos without giving into corruption, are struggling with the implications of the so-called Age of Sigmar.  Since the Azyrites burst back into the Realm of Fire, promising to reistablish civilisation, after fleeing to hide in Azyr while the dark forces ruled the realms, things haven't exactly been great.

On the face of it, Sigmarite devotees trying to reclaim the realms from the Dark Gods is a good thing, right?  But like a bunch of hipsters moving into a run-down, inner-city neighbourhood bringing with them their overpriced coffee shops, artisan beard barbers and yoga boutiques, the Azyrites carve out a nice little life for themselves at the expense of the Aqshyan locals, many of whom are no longer able to afford to live in their ancestral homeland because the cost of housing, food and, most importantly, booze, has increased so much.

Heldanarr Fall is a shit-farmer who has just about had enough of all this.  He sees the injustice that has befallen his people at the hands of the Azyrites, and watches as his people’s quality of life declines year on year.

He and his sister, Varrianala (Varry), are reduced to collecting the droppings, or magnure, of the areas native lavamanders, which they sell to the city’s wealthy to heat their homes with. To Fall, there is little difference between the followers of Chaos and the denizens of Order; both seek to rob him and his people of all they have, they just have different ways of doing it. All gods are let downs, no matter that pantheon they belong to.

But at least the Fall siblings have each other. When you don’t have a lot of much else (other than piles of lavamander shit) family becomes very important. Mind you, Heldanarr Fall is in short supply of that too. All of his other siblings and his father were killed years ago by Beasts of Chaos, and his mother (allegedly) ascended into the ranks of Sigmar’s Stormcast Eternals. All Fall has left in the world is his sister.

Beasts of Chaos army for the Michigan GT. Credit: Michael O "Muggins"

It is a grim existence, the forces of Chaos assaulting on one side and Azyrite exploitation on the other. Fall is trapped in the pressure cooker of circumstance; heated by the trauma of loss and the indignancy of injustice, as well as by the ambient fury of Aqshy, it is no wonder that he eventually embarks upon the most iconic of Warhammer of journeys… the Path to Glory.

This may be the best Path to Glory novel I have read, an in-depth and expansive exploration of the champion’s journey to corruption and victory. It details a journey that is more than just ‘I want more power so I’m going to devote myself to the dark gods, get myself a crab arm or whatever, and then go kill some good guys.’  Fall’s fall to the dark side is nuanced, tragic and, above all, deeply human.

He is a fascinating character with strong principles and values. But like anyone hoping to forge a path according to their conscience, he has to constantly reevaluate and recalibrate his ethics to fit the twisted reality in which he finds himself. He is highly driven, justice seeking, at times unflinchingly uncompromising, whilst at other times strangely compassionate. At some points in the book he is a bloodthirsty warlord, at other times an idealistic socialist revolutionary. He has a vision for his homeland where there is no exploitation or oppression, where there isn’t even currency, yet at the same time rivers literally run red with the blood he spills. The contradictions and dichotomies are rife, but such is the nature of the Path to Glory.

The Azyrites make for compelling villains in this story. Lady Lellen Se Roye is the viceroy-regent of Candip, Fall’s gentrified hometown. She is a greedy, corrupt and arrogant antagonist and her sister, the priestess Elene, is an entitled, elitist and effortlessly hate-able Sigmarite priestess. They are perfectly emblematic of Fall’s struggle, and are very effective at making you immediately want to fall into ranks behind him.  Even the city’s Stormcast Eternal Lord Imperatant, Ildrid Stormsworn of the Hammers of Sigmar, cannot stand the Se Royes and does everything she can do to halt their ambitions, doing her best to delay Candip's anointing as an official City of Sigmar.

Anyone who is fed up of getting shafted by their landlord, taken advantage of by their employer, or ripped off by wanky cafés, cannot help but have some sympathy for Fall. For a book set in a fantasy realm of fire, its themes are startlingly relatable.

But the forces of Order aren’t the only bad guys in this story. Chaos is an ever-present threat, and Fall knows this. Despite beginning to ally himself with he dark gods (while convincing himself he’s not), Fall will never forget that it was the Beastmen who were the ones who killed his family. Despite disappearing from the AOS game, they still serve as a really great reminder of the visceral, primal state of Chaos.  This makes for a great metaphor for what is going on within Fall, as he battles inwardly against the warping anger and compulsions within himself.

Blades of Khorne Blood Warriors. Credit: Rich Nutter

And then, of course, there is Khorne, the Blood God, the Godeater, constantly looking over Fall’s shoulder and inviting him to pledge himself to the dark gods and receive their boons; always seeking to corrupt his bloodlust and desire for martial greatness, vengeance and justice. Nguyen does a really great job of describing the wars on the battlefield, but he also portrays this battle for Fall’s soul really compellingly as well.

Naturally, following the Path to Glory will also bring you into contact with other warlords on their own intersecting paths.

Most prominent is Kaddarar the Seeker, a fully devoted follower of the Godeater.  She is a zealous and totally single-minded blade of Khorne.  And she’s also a bit sexy. Apparently. Turns out blood-crazed murder-barbarian is just the kind of woman Fall would swipe right for. As well as some hints of sexual tension between the two characters, you also have the tension that Kaddarar has promised to one day kill or be killed by Fall. As Chaos warps Fall’s notions of justice and fairness, so it also warps his notion of romance and love.

Boskin is also a really great character that Fall bumps into along the way.  He’s kind of portrayed as a bit of a lovable rogue, ducking and diving, not to be trusted, Del-Boy-esque. Motivated on the whole by greed, but not in a two-dimensional way, his Path is a fascinating one to watch unfold as Chaos warps his desires.

Yron is a mystic and devotee of the Chaos cult. Her path to glory is one that takes the course of rituals and rites.  She balances Fall’s determination not to have anything to do with any of the gods at all, and offers his followers faith where he rejects it. There is also Tominer, a Khornite priestess, who crops up from time to time and serves as an interesting vehicle for the book’s theology (another thing Nguyen does really well).

Jujjar is an old friend of Fall, well before he ever became the Godeater’s Son. He has a very different idea of where their movement should be going, and his own Path to Glory does not fit comfortably alongside Fall's, providing plenty of opportunity for narrative bumps along the way.

Indeed, Fall’s whole inner circle are a mishmash of diverse and antagonistic personalities, and it is his job to try to hold them all in tension, just as he has to unite the multitude of tribes, warbands and peoples that form his growing kingdom. Of course, none of this is quite as hard as the task Fall has of trying to hold together all of the disparate voices and desires within himself.

Even Fall’s horse, Micaw, an old clapped-out nag, is on her own Path to Glory of sorts.  Fall was originally planning to eat the horse at one point in the book, but he decides to spare her and use her for transportation instead. Now, with every unnatural mutation/boon the steed receives, shaping it more and more away from its original station as a beast of burden and towards its new form as a monstrous, reptilian, carnivorous war steed, we see a parallel with Fall’s own unnatural transformation.

What is actually really interesting about Fall is that he actually has a very hard time killing people once he gets to know them – which could be seen as a bit of deficiency in a warlord. Even his old nag was spared from becoming meat. This is a really fascinating dynamic in the book, and even becomes a key driving force in the sequel, Blood of the Godeater.

Ultimately, I’m not sure I have read such a thorough and interesting character study in an AOS novel. We all know the main thrust of Warhammer is often to say “there are no good guys, everyone’s a bit evil” but this book goes beyond that and says “here’s a human being, and he’s struggling with many of the things you, the reader, are struggling with, and actually he’s quite likeable sometimes, and identifiable, I think you might actually quite like him. Oh, but now he’s eating human flesh.”

All of this is coupled with the fact that Nguyen is really very good at putting words on a page, often slipping in little chunks of philosophy or observations about human behaviour that you don’t quite expect to find in a Warhammer book.

Garrek's Reavers. Credit: Magos Sockbert

There are some really good pieces of writing, and some delicious irony. Fall wears his father’s death mask throughout the book, all the time descending deeper towards the powers that claimed his father’s life. At the same time, Fall’s mother was rumoured to have been snatched up as a Stormcast Eternal, leaving behind the family she was supposedly trying to protect, exposing one of the greatest tragedies that religion can inflict upon a person; when a parent puts the love of their god ahead of the love of their own children. The result of this mother’s devotion to Order is that her son goes on to become a powerful Chaos warlord.

There’s one scene which is masterfully done, and I think symbolizes much of the whole book. Fall comes face to face with Ildrid Stormsworn, the Lord Imperitant, and they have a big fight. But while fighting they both try to get under each other’s skin and unravel the other mentally at the same time. They’re poking and prodding at each other’s psyche, trying to get the measure of the other – but they’re both doing so while hiding behind unexpressive masks. The book is richly layered, and makes the point very well that humans are too.

As far as world building goes, the book isn’t going to offer you a huge amount of general Age of Sigmar lore, it is mostly focused on the little corner of Aqshy in which it is set. There are some tidbits of Slaves to Darkness and Khorne lore, and a bit of Beasts of Chaos and Cities of Sigmar, but not a huge amount.

Urkhan the Dark Warden. Credit: Rich Nutter

However, the book really does build its own little narrative universe beautifully.  Strange mountains that lead to the Realm of Chaos, up-side-down cities hanging off the bottom of the world, ancient states and frontier towns, all trying to survive in the extreme heat of the Realm of Fire.  I really got a sense of place within the book, even if I did have to concentrate quite hard to remember all of the names and characteristics of the different tribes and peoples.

This book feels like a sweeping epic, but also like a detailed character piece. It tells the story of an empire being born, and of a soul being damned at the same time. Once you’ve read this book, you really know you’ve read it. Heldanarr Fall has stayed with me for a long time since I’ve finished. Ive thought about him a lot. I think this book is going to take its place as a classic Age of Sigmar book, and now I’m really looking forward to getting stuck into the sequel.

title: Games Workshop scraps Necromunda RPG a month after announcing it
content:
Games Workshop just dropped a bombshell. It will not be producing a Warhammer Necromunda tabletop RPG after all. The only explanation? "We've decided to focus our efforts on providing even more great minis for the core game". Oh… okay.

This has obviously caused quite a stir, and it must be said, is pretty odd. GW only announced Necromunda Roleplay a month ago, in a since-deleted Warhammer Community article published September 18. But you can't hide from the WayBackMachine, friends. We see you.

Necromunda Roleplay used a d100 system, and would've come with minis and prebuilt character sheets for an Escher Assassin, Orlock Gunslinger, Squat Fixer, or Goliath Champion PC - while also letting you build your own ganger from any of the six main Clan Houses. It was designed to be a mini-based RPG, compatible with the full Necromunda range, and with 18 minis included in the release box.

This wasn't just a far-off plan that GW decided not to go ahead with. They had lots of product shots ready, a very clear idea of what was in the core set box - right down to the rulebook page count - and promised a release date 'soon'. It seems likely this thing was ready to hit shelves before Christmas.

The sudden cancellation is a bolt from the blue, and speculation is rife, while hard facts are in short supply. People keep pointing to Cubicle 7, but in a Facebook post a few weeks ago, they said they've never had the Necromunda license. Truth is: we don't really know what happened here.

The cancellation will obviously be upsetting for tabletop RPG fans, but for those who really do just care about the minis, GW assures that those that were announced with Necromunda Roleplay will still be getting made. It's revealed a new roadmap for 2027 in fact. Here's that:

  • Spring 2027: Some Mad Max fun, a return to the Ash Wastes and WarCom teases "the biggest plastic vehicle kit yet" for Necromunda.
  • Summer 2027: Hive Secundus again, for grimy Malstrain Genestealer goodness.
  • Autumn 2027: 'Underhive Brutes' for the original six houses - teaser art shows a Luther pattern 'Ambot'
  • Winter 2027: Bounty hunters

Looks cool, but personally I'm way too distracted by the surprise cancellation just 35 days after the game was announced, to think much about that right now.

What happened? Share your wild theories with us over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: Greenwood is a huge hit at Essen Spiel, but is this new board game worth the hype?
content:
On opening day of Essen Spiel, board game fans queued around corners to get a glimpse of Greenwood. The rebellious fantasy strategy title has been hyped to high heaven online, and boy, did gamers show up to see what the fuss was about. I sat down for one of the new game's first demos to see if the hype was deserved.

What first grabbed me was the theme. Greenwood is, on the surface, a quaint fantasy game where you ramble the titular forests, taking in nature and cavorting with cutesy creatures. In reality, it's a guerilla act of sabotage. The adorable inhabitants of Greenwood are held there against their will, and you're here to rescue them.

Like all great strategy games, Greenwood is a cluster of interconnected engines. They seem imposing at first glance, but you fall into rhythm very quickly.

Each round begins at Dusk, when you choose three of four possible perks: play a companion card onto your board, place a protection token on a threat card, discard a card to move up the Aurora track, and/or increase your Strength.

Already, I've thrown a lot of concepts at you. Let's break them down.

Your hand of cards represents many things. When played onto your board, they are allies who can aid you with unique abilities. To activate said powers, you'll place an Energy token on the card during the Night phase. You also have Spy tokens that copy the power of opponents' companions, but generally, it's one token per card. The same goes for Hiking tokens, which are placed on your cards to take a Move/Map action rather than activate their ability.

Now, onto Protection tokens. The Druids who rule Greenwood become increasingly suspicious of your sabotage as the nights go on. This is represented by a Threat track, which gains more cards with each round. Threat cards offer penalties when placing your Spy token, but Protection tokens negate this - and get you a nice extra bonus to boot.

Next, let's talk about the tracks. Strength represents your physical might. It grants various bonuses as you ascend, and it opens additional slots for Knowledge tokens. You collect these via a Study action and by discarding cards to gather your desired tokens. More on these tokens later.

Similar to Strength, the main board has a Wayfinder track that offers bonuses for investing in it. This might be anything from points to cards to Energy tokens. Basically, these are your two 'engine-building' tracks, designed to unlock additional, more powerful turns. You can up your Wayfinder track in all sorts of ways, from visiting specific places on the map to improving your other tracks.

The last track to track (somebody stop me) is your Aurora. After a simultaneous Dusk phase, everyone takes Departure actions equal to their Aurora value. That might mean removing Hiking tokens from cards or using specific powers called Spells. There's some base Spells available to everyone, but companions often offer more.

After that, Night falls, and the rescue mission begins. You'll take turns placing a Hiking token, Energy, or Spy on companions until you choose or have to pass.

So far, Greenwood sounds like a game of pushing tracks as high as they go. It sort of is, but there's a point to it that makes this more than just a spreadsheet.

The ultimate goal is to rescue those aforementioned cuddly critters. You'll collect and discard their matching Knowledge tokens, move to their space on the map, and sweep them to the safety of your personal submarine. Suddenly, your refugees are transformed into tetrominoes. These must be carefully slotted into your cramped sub, with placement rewards for filling columns and slots. It's very Feast for Odin, though Greenwood is nowhere near as complex.

Perhaps that easy comparison is, for me, the difference between 'liking' and 'loving' Greenwood. It's impressive how seamless everything feels, don't get me wrong. Greenwood is a well-oiled strategic machine that glides as smooth as a stealthy submarine. It manages to be challenging without off-putting. For all it's decision points, turns move quickly, with very little to trip you up and gum its gears.

But it's nothing we haven't seen before. Perhaps a full game - or several - would reveal to me Greenwood's idiosyncrasies. I can only give my first impression: a strategy game whose tried-and-tested mechanics work flawlessly, but feel rather too safe.

I have my issues too with the theme, the very thing that drew me to Greenwood in the first place. It's unique and well-realized by the game's lovely art and production. However, I don't fully understand why a covert rescue mission is a competitive endeavor.

Surely, as vigilantes with a shared goal, we'd want to work together? Why are we spying on each other and quibbling over who gets to be the 'best' rescuer? Greenwood presents a thrilling story about a fight for freedom, but it never really commits to telling that story with its mechanics.

I'd love to play Greenwood again. There's an engaging engine here worth exploring. But, for me, it wasn't an instant buy.

Want to learn more about Essen's best games? Check out our coverage from the show floor, posted in the Wargamer Discord. Or, check out our best board games guide for this year's top titles.

title: Old Faerie MTG card spikes 530% thanks to underrated competitive combos
content:
The Shadowmoor Magic: The Gathering card Knacksaw Clique is getting seriously expensive. Regular copies have gone from $2.80 back in August, to over $18 today. Meanwhile, foils have been selling for as much as $200, even if they're not in mint condition. TCGPlayer lists very few sales for these foil Cliques, incidentally, suggesting the supply is already pretty low.

As a rare card from an older set, and a faerie at that, this card was always liable to spike if the right synergies came along. It seems like its time is here, but surprisingly the format that seems responsible for this spike is actually cEDH - not where we normally look for big market drivers.

Even weirder, there's no new cards at all making this one spike. Instead, it's an infinite combo that already existed, but seems to have been undervalued up until now. However, in the last few months Kinnan, Bonder Prodigy decks featuring Knacksaw Clique have topped several cEDH tournaments, including the 80-player Topdeck Invitational back in August.

Since Knacksaw Clique has an untap ability, it's fairly easy to make its ability go infinite. You just need a way to make the creature tap for mana. With Paradise Mantle equipped or Cryptolith Rites on the board, Knacksaw Clique can tap for one blue mana, and with Kinnan in play that becomes two. Then you're free to mill all of your opponents down to nothing.

The combo is very versatile, with multiple cards that can make it work. For instance, you can use it even if Kinnan isn't available, with a card like Training Grounds to reduce the activated ability cost to one, which then means you don't need his mana doubling.

While it's not new, it seems fans have gained a new appreciation for the combo, or perhaps someone just decided to buy out the supply after the tournament wins? What's funny to me is that people have been calling Knacksaw Clique underrated for quite literally a decade.

Either way, if the hype dies down we might expect to see its price fall somewhat, but given how few copies are around, it'll probably remain fairly expensive if it doesn't get an eventual reprint.

title: Folk horror miniature skirmish game sees pilgrims fighting with faith
content:
Set in "a new world that was never meant to be found", Pilgrim: The Haunted Frontier is a folk horror miniature skirmish game where players work together, controlling pilgrims fending off terrifying monsters in the woods. With the game's first scenario out now for free and a Gamefound crowdfunder on the way, we spoke to the designer (and Buer Games cofounder) Eric Michael Robinson to find out more.

"I only want to make games with worlds I really want to dive deep into," Robinson says. Buer's other titles - Carnivore, set in the desperate cataclysm of the end-Cretaceous mass extinction, and 1490 Doom, set in a medieval apocalypse - go hard on aesthetics, and Pilgrim is no exception. It's also, like the others, not a cheery game.

"There's something compelling about a group of people leaving home to cross an ocean to start a new life in a new land," says Robinson. "The game's goal is to immerse the player in a really fun experience exploring an unknown land filled with terrifying horrors. There's mystery, discovery, side plots, and really spooky minis. I love playing cooperative games and this felt like a great setting for solo or co-op play."

Instead of HP, the key stats for surviving the dangers of Pilgrim is Faith. The demo scenario sees players contending with shades on the seashore, who can drain a pilgrim's faith just by getting close. Lose it all, and there's a ticking clock before that character is lost to madness. And since there are only seven named pilgrims in the game, all with unique abilities, that's probably not a good thing.

"The faith mechanic is very prominent as the Pilgrims go deeper into the woods and experience more horrors," says the creator. "They use Faith to reroll failed rolls but Pilgrims must be careful not to use it all, or they become susceptible to drifting into the woods and being claimed."

While the game's Wendigo (who appears on the front cover) reminds us of the beast from The Ritual, Robinson gives a surprising source when asked for media that inspired the game: Over the Garden Wall. "That show is perfect in my opinion. That idea of the unknown very much influenced the mystery of Pilgrim's world."

Eric says Pilgrim shares some similarities with Joseph McCollough's Rangers of Shadow Deep, another co-op skirmish game where you venture into the dark with a band of cohorts, but says the two have very different mechanics.

With immersion-setting music and evocative art and minis, the Pilgrim looks set to be a truly spooky game. We don't yet have a release date or Gamefound launch, though Buer Games has a preview event planned for October 28.

Come join the Wargamer Discord to chat more about this game and many like it!

title: D&D reveals new batch of monsters designed by kids
content:
After a three year gap, Wizards of the Coast has revealed Volume Two of Misplaced Monsters, a miniature menagerie of D&D monsters designed by miniature humans: or, as they're often called, children.

Releasing on December 2, 2026, Misplaced Monsters: Vol 2 is a collection of eight monsters designed to support a charity, with all proceeds "100% of the sales price" going to Seattle Children's Hospital's mental and behavioral health programs.

A relatively small expansion, the volume contains eight monsters and one magic item and is priced at $7.95. Like the old Extra Life Magic: The Gathering Secret Lairs, a major part of the appeal (apart from giving to charity) is that you get to see the children's art side by side with professional artists' recreations of that art.

In fact, Wizards has shared the pics on social media, so we can see exactly what is in this product. There's an interesting mix: some blobs, a dire elephant seal, and 'Minnie' who looks like a regular cat, but presumably is not.

Here's the full list of monsters:

  • Elea the Monster
  • Dire Elephant Seal
  • Minnie
  • Octo-Plus
  • Retanglosaurus
  • Pengu-Z
  • Chroapicosoa
  • Monster Ball

No clues have been given about the magic item though.

If this lot are anything like the batch of Misplaced Monsters from 2023, which included a dragon that dealt blueberry damage, there'll be plenty of weirdness in here. You can also buy the two packs together, for 14 monsters in total.

title: This is MTG Universes Beyond's laziest trick and I hate it
content:
At the Magic: The Gathering Star Trek debut on Monday, there were several cards I liked, and one that made me roll my eyes so hard I may have actually damaged something. That card was Seven of Nine, Unassimilated, and I bet you can already guess why I don't like it.

Yes, it's the transformation ability that gives her a 7/9 statline that irks me. The rest of the card is absolutely fine. She's got an ability related to differently named lands, representing exploration, and she loots, representing accumulated knowledge. Then she gets stronger from all that exploration, I guess. It doesn't have much to do with Seven of Nine's journey in particular, I think, and would arguably work for literally any Star Trek character with a story arc, but ho hum.

I'm in danger of making a mountain out of a molehill here, but I just find Magic's habit of spotting a number in a character's name and then building the card around that number so damn dull. It feels lazy, corny even, and makes it seem like the designers are just phoning it in.

They've done it so many times now, too. From the Ten Rings to Doctor Octopus, Eleven to The Fantastic Four, and I hate it every single time. This isn't even the only example in this set - they also gave Deep Space 9, 9/9 stats and a station and mana cost of 9.

At its best, Universes Beyond incorporates and adapts the characteristics of our favorite franchises into the game system that is Magic: The Gathering. From a Weeping Angel becoming a harmless artifact when you play a creature to Boromir sacrificing himself to save your other creatures, it feels great to see these moments and characters thoughtfully encapsulated on a card.

I don't mind when they get cute with it, either, like using reminder text so Shadowfax can show us the meaning of haste or the split-second mechanic to represent pausing the game so you can do some Fallout Inventory Management.

But just slapping numbers onto stuff doesn't do this. Seven of Nine's character has nothing to do with the numbers seven and nine, just as Eleven's character has nothing to do with the number 11. I really don't see who this is for. Surely this doesn't please fans of the character or Magic fans. The joke is overplayed, no one thinks it's clever anymore

I genuinely would prefer this card if it was exactly the same, but became an 8/8 instead.

title: MTG Commander banlist 2026
content:
Looking for the MTG Commander banlist? Commander is a vast, powerful, and ever-changing format, so it's crucial to stay on top of card bans. If you need a quick reminder of which cards can and can't go in your favorite deck, here's a complete list of Commander bans, from the latest to the very first.

So far, there have been 83 banned cards in MTG's Commander format. Use the links below to check out the latest changes and updates; the full banlist; or Wizards' new system of Game Changers and play brackets in EDH, explained. For more bans in other formats, see our full MTG banlist tracker.

  • Latest Commander banlist update
  • Full Commander banlist
  • Game Changers list
  • Brackets explained

Latest Commander banlist update

On February 9, 2026, Wizards of the Coast unbanned two Commander cards:

  • Biorhythm
  • Lutri, the Spellchaser (except as Companion)

Lutri's case is obvious - it was only banned because it could serve as a Companion in any deck.

The decision to make a new designation 'banned as Companion' appeared to weigh heavily on the designers, based on Gavin Verhey's article - adding sub-lists increases complexity and the chance that players will bring a card in a slot it's not supposed to. The decision was deemed acceptable because the worst case scenario for player mistakes isn't that bad - you tell the player with Lutri in the companion slot that he's banned, and they drop him into the 99.

Because Lutri was banned for reasons not really related to power he bypassed the gamechangers list, where unbanned cards typically go.

Meanwhile, Biorhythm was unbanned following a trend of unbanning expensive, high-impact cards that have a big impact on the game. If Worldfire and Coalition Victory can be legal cards without messing up the format too much, so can Biorhythm.

Full Commander banlist

(8 of) The Power 9

  • Ancestral Recall - banned April 2005
  • Black Lotus - banned April 2005
  • Mox Emerald - banned April 2005
  • Mox Jet - banned April 2005
  • Mox Pearl - banned April 2005
  • Mox Ruby - banned April 2005
  • Mox Sapphire - banned April 2005
  • Time Walk - banned April 2005

It's no surprise to see these here. If any card was going to be banned in Commander, it would be the Power 9 - some of the most broken cards ever made in Magic, each offering absurd value for their mana cost.

Speaking of cost, what's interesting is that it was their price point, not their power level, that originally saw these cards consigned to the Commander banlist - in the very first spate of bannings back in 2005.

The RC was worried that these cards would auto-includes for anyone wanting a really strong deck, and didn't want the fan-made format to have a perceived budget of thousands of dollars.

You might notice only 8/9ths of the Power 9 is actually banned. Timetwister is really an honorary member of the gang - it's busted when played with cards from the other 8. But in fact, a wheel, even a really great wheel like Timetwister, isn't worth making a fuss about.

Broken in the format

  • Limited Resources - banned June 2008
  • Channel - banned April 2005
  • Fastbond - banned June 2009
  • Trade Secrets - banned April 2013
  • Griselbrand - banned June 2012
  • Karakas - banned September 2008
  • Lutri, the Spellchaser - banned as companion February 2026
  • Yawgmoth's Bargain - banned May 2006

These cards are all banned because their designs are unbalanced in the context of EDH. Some, like Channel and Yawgmoth's Bargain, use life as a resource - one that's far more abundant when you start on 40. Others work poorly with multiple players. For instance, Trade Secrets allows two players to collude against the others for a runaway advantage, while Limited Resources stops anyone playing more than two to three lands.

Finally, Lutri is only banned as a companion - because the singleton nature of the format means he could (and therefore, optimally, should) be a companion for any red/blue deck.

It's almost refreshing to see these designs - memories of a time before every card was designed for Commander.

Dexterity cards

  • Chaos Orb - banned June 2010
  • Falling Star - banned April 2005

These feel more like unset cards, and wouldn't be printed without the acorn stamp today. The RC didn't want cards that relied on manual dexterity, so for the sake of both accessibility and convenience, these were banned.

  • Balance - banned April 2005
  • Dockside Extortionist - banned September 2024
  • Emrakul, the Aeons Torn - banned December 2010
  • Erayo, Soratami Ascendant - banned September 2014
  • Flash - banned April 2020
  • Golos, Tireless Pilgrim - banned September 2021
  • Hullbreacher - banned July 2021
  • Iona, Shield of Emeria - banned July 2019
  • Jeweled Lotus - banned September 2024
  • Leovold, Emissary of Trest - banned April 2017
  • Library of Alexandria - banned April 2005
  • Mana Crypt - banned September 2024
  • Nadu, Winged Wisdom - banned September 2024
  • Paradox Engine - banned July 2019
  • Primeval Titan - banned September 2012
  • Prophet of Kruphix - banned January 2016
  • Recurring Nightmare - banned February 2008
  • Rofellos, Llanowar Emissary - banned September 2014
  • Shahrazad - banned September 2011
  • Sundering Titan - banned June 2012
  • Sylvan Primordial - banned February 2014
  • Time Vault - banned December 2008
  • Tinker - banned March 2009
  • Tolarian Academy - banned June 2010
  • Upheaval - banned April 2005

Conspiracy cards

25 cards with the Conspiracy type are banned in Commander and all other formats. The full list of Conspiracy cards banned in Commander is:

  • Adriana's Valor
  • Advantageous Proclamation
  • Assemble the Rank and Vile
  • Backup Plan
  • Brago's Favor
  • Double Stroke
  • Echoing Boon
  • Emissary's Ploy
  • Hired Heist
  • Hold the Perimeter
  • Hymn of the Wilds
  • Immediate Action
  • Incendiary Dissent
  • Iterative Analysis
  • Muzzio's Preparations
  • Natural Unity
  • Power Play
  • Secret Summoning
  • Secrets of Paradise
  • Sentinel Dispatch
  • Sovereign's Realm
  • Summoner's Bond
  • Unexpected Potential
  • Weight Advantage
  • Worldknit

Ante cards

Nine cards that reference 'playing for ante' are banned in Commander and all other formats. This is because they don't work within the rules. Playing for keeps in a four-player game is probably a bad bet anyhow. The banned MTG ante cards are:

  • Amulet of Quoz
  • Bronze Tablet
  • Contract from Below
  • Darkpact
  • Demonic Attorney
  • Jewelled Bird
  • Rebirth
  • Tempest Efreet
  • Timmerian Fiends

Offensive cards

The Commander banlist includes cards that are racially or culturally insensitive. These cards have been banned in all formats, and their images were even removed from Wizards of the Coast's database in 2020. The seven cards currently included in this ban are:

  • Invoke Prejudice
  • Cleanse
  • Stone-Throwing Devils
  • Pradesh Gypsies
  • Jihad
  • Imprison
  • Crusade

Game Changers list

In 2025, Wizards of the Coast introduced a separate but linked 'Game Changers' list to the banlist conversation. Game Changers are cards that dramatically warp a game when (or shortly after) they're played. The number of game changers a deck contains is one factor in determining which Commander 'bracket' it falls into during pre-game discussions.

Though certainly not banned - or even at risk of banning - Wizards has made it clear that future banned cards are likely to come from this list. Similarly, any cards that get unbanned are likely to move onto the Game Changers list.

Wizards of the Coast last updated the Game Changers list along with the latest Commander banlist update on February 9, 2026.

Current Game Changers list

  • Biorhythm

Brackets explained

The beta brackets system is a tool to help Commander players talk about the gameplay experience they want to create with their deck. Each bracket has a set of deck-building conditions: if a deck meets those conditions, it sits in that bracket.

1. Exhibition

Decks prioritize theme over function and showcase a unique idea or experience over valuing winning.

  • No game changers
  • No mass land denial
  • No extra turns
  • No two-card infinite combos (game-enders, lockouts, or infinite)
  • Few tutors

2. Core

Decks are focused, even if every card choice isn't the highest power, and comparable to an average precon. Wins are often telegraphed or incremental.

  • No game changers
  • No mass land denial
  • No chaining extra turns
  • No two-card infinite combos (game-enders, lockouts, or infinite)
  • Few tutors

3. Upgraded

Decks are thoughtfully designed, full of synergistic or strong cards. Games could end out of nowhere with powerful spells and late-game combos.

  • No mass land denial
  • No chaining extra turns
  • Late game, two-card infinite combos allowed
  • Up to three game changers

4. Optimized

Decks are turbocharged with the most powerful cards in the format. Everybody intends to win and is ready to play against anything.

No restrictions other than the banlist.

5. CEDH

Decks are built to win in the competitive metagame. Players intend to use only the most powerful strategies.

  • No restrictions other than the banlist.

Are Commander brackets power levels?

Commander brackets are numbered, but these numbers don't measure the power level of a deck. The higher the bracket, the more tools the deck has to succeed in competitive, meta-focused gameplay. The lower the bracket, the more casual and focused on 'doing something neat with friends' the deck is.

Hopefully, players can use the brackets to choose decks that have similar gameplay goals. There will still be decks that perform well above or below what their bracket suggests.

You'll find a welcoming community in the free Wargamer Discord who are eager to discuss your latest deck brews with you. To make sure you don't miss the best stories on Wargamer each week, sign up to our newsletter.

title: MTG Star Trek breaks one of Magic's most infamous combos
content:
Oh good, MTG players found a way to break Food Chain! This classic combo seen in Legacy and cEDH decks is about to get even stronger, thanks to a brand new card from the Star Trek set. That card features Khan, one of the franchise's most iconic villains.

Khan, Wrathful Heart is a legendary creature that can be cast from exile, which immediately makes it an obvious choice for Food Chain decks. For those unfamiliar, this combo relies on Food Chain, alongside any creature that can be cast from exile - such as Misthollow Griffin or Squee. You keep on sacrificing those creatures to Food Chain and recasting them, with a net gain of one mana each time, allowing you to make infinite mana with which to win the game.

What makes Khan, Wrathful Heart so much better than these older options is that he has another effect. He can also turn creatures or artifacts into card draw. Traditionally, for a Food Chain cEDH deck, you've needed to run a commander that provides immediate value from entering the battlefield (be that card draw or direct damage) so you can keep casting and exiling it with your unlimited mana and have a built in way to win.

Pantlaza or Atraxa, cards that fetch up other cards on ETB, are classic examples of Food Chain commanders in this vein.

Khan provides that value all by himself, though, which means technically any deck can now be a Food Chain deck. You can't actually whiff as long as your commander is a creature, since you can sacrifice them to Khan if you don't draw anything you want to put in the bin. Remember you have infinite mana in this scenario; commander tax may as well not exist.

I'm excited to see what black-based Food Chain decks crop up around Khan, and if this widens the pool of commanders folks are using for this archetype.

title: The Pokémon TCG's first 2027 release, Flowing Fists, is revealed
content:
We finally know the name of the next Pokémon TCG set coming out after Delta Reign. That set is Flowing Fists, and it's launching on February 5, 2027. We've long known that this release will focus on Mega Lucario, specifically the new version - Mega Lucario Z - which debuted in the Pokémon Legends Z-A Mega Dimension DLC last December.

Flowing Fists is the English language counterpart to Aura Seeker, the Japanese set due to launch November 27 this year. We've already seen several of its cards, including the face card Mega Lucario, and with the set roughly a month away, we should expect The Pokémon Company to release the Japanese spoilers imminently, giving the rest of us a sneak peek at what to expect in February.

Obviously, it's the full art rares we're all looking forward to seeing, but even before we knew what this set would be called, a couple of its cards had already been shown off. As mentioned, these include Mega Lucario Z, a metal type Mega ex Pokémon with an 'Aura Seeker' ability that fetches up any Supporter from your deck. It can also easily KO weak exs, as its 120 damage attack deals twice as much to them.

However, even though it only has 210 HP, Mega Lucario Z ex still can't take down the new Sigilyph ex. That's because it has an ability that blocks all damage from mega evolutions. While this only prevents damage to itself, this wall is still likely to be a meta-shaping tool, helping to keep mega evolution decks in check. Perhaps it'll be a boon to the powerful single-prize strategies that are already performing well.

Before Flowing Fists, we still have the final Pokémon set of the year, Delta Reign, to look forward to, as it launches on November 6 - just a couple of weeks away. If you haven't already, check out the chase cards from this release, from the beautiful Raikou ex to the surprisingly pretty Kecleon.

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. The Traveler’s Handbook introduces eight origins, four classes with two subclasses each, and six powerful Traveler Dynasties that serve as in-game factions. The Exodus Encyclopedia packs in stat blocks for constructs, Celestials, changelings, awakened beings, and human NPCs, along with Remnant items for research and combat.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.
